Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4461 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stocks were slammed on Friday, closing out a brutal week for markets as the much-hyped Anthropic IPO caused investors to take profits on the artificial intelligence-led rally rather than revive it.
  • Sources indicate that the tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 5.28% to close at 22,617.73.
  • The Nasdaq-100 plummeted 5.6% and entered a bear market on an intraday basis, down 20% from its recent high.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stocks were slammed on Friday, closing out a brutal week for markets as the much-hyped Anthropic IPO caused investors to take profits on the artificial intelligence-led rally rather than revive it. The Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year, and the S&P 500 entered correction territory alongside the Dow Jones Industrial Average.

Sources indicate that the tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 5.28% to close at 22,617.73. The index was down 2.7% year to date. The broad market S&P 500 dropped 3.7% to end at 6,910.39, while the blue-chip Dow fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33. Both the S&P 500 and Dow moved 10% below their closing records.

The Nasdaq-100 plummeted 5.6% and entered a bear market on an intraday basis, down 20% from its recent high.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic lost 8.5%, giving back a large chunk of its 17% jump in its Nasdaq debut Thursday and pressuring the broader AI trade. Chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia slid more than 13% and around 14%, respectively. Nvidia saw selling pressure increase after Reuters reported that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring possible accounting concerns at the tech giant. It also recorded its longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis. Micron Technology dropped almost 14%.

Those declines in tech built on the losses seen in Thursday's horrid session, where the major averages each lost more than 2%, and the Dow closing below the key 50,000 level for the first time since June.

"This is not just a valuation-driven correction. It's becoming broader," said Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon. "Right now, it's definitely risk-off.".

Recent findings suggest that the losses are alarming investors who were hopeful that Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO would revive enthusiasm for the AI trade. Now, the market looks to be on the cusp of a true capitulation after getting roiled in recent weeks with a series of negative headlines. Signs of moderation in the capital expenditures splurge, Democratic wins in the 2026 midterms and Jensen Huang's ouster at Nvidia all raised questions about the future of the AI buildout.

On top of that, the potential for more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve is spooking traders as well.

Industry observers note that investors hid out in defensive areas of the market, with retailers such as Walmart and Costco as well as others like Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble seeing gains. Walmart gained more than 1%, while Costco, Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble each rose around 1%.

"The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth," said Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners.

In a recent development, for the week, the Dow fell 8%, notching its worst weekly performance since March 2020. The Nasdaq finished down about 10%, also posting its largest one-week pullback in more than six years. The S&P 500 decreased 8.6%, seeing its worst week since April 2025 in the wake of President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs announcement.

The three leading U.S. indexes experienced a massive sell-off on Friday.

According to recent reports, the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% to close at 6,910.39, while the Nasdaq Composite plummeted 5.28% to 22,617.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33.

All three major averages were trading below their 200-day moving averages on Friday, and BTIG believes more turmoil could be ahead.

"Generally speaking once something is below a 200 DMA, the risk is to the downside," stated Jonathan Krinsky, the firm's chief market technician.

Thursday marked the sixth consecutive day of declines for the S&P 500, and Krinsky found that over the last 30 years, there are only three prior instances of six-day losing streaks that close below the 200-day moving average but not by more than 3%.

According to recent reports, "The 'slightly' good news is that all three saw SPX higher five days later. The not so good news is that all of them saw meaningful downside after that small pop," he said.

When assessing Thursday's performance, Wolfe Research found that the broad market index's "violent" reversal after its attempt to move back to its 200-day moving average at the open was succeeded by the "worst breadth reading" since last December, seeing decliners outnumber advancers by 12:1.

"Broken trends and deteriorating momentum remain significant headwinds," wrote technical analyst Rob Ginsberg in a Thursday note. "The bulls need to mount a powerful defense here to stabilize the market and begin reversing the broader deterioration.".

The national average for regular gasoline fell to $3.69 a gallon on Friday, down from $3.72 on Thursday, according to AAA. Prices are still about 59 cents higher than a year ago.

The drop comes ahead of Thanksgiving next week, with 73 million people expected to take road trips.

"It's possible the national average will drop another 15 cents by next Thursday and avoid setting a new record," according to AAA's post.

Industry observers note that brent ​crude futures, the international benchmark, were up 0.64% to $92.57 a barrel on Friday, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December rose 0.93% to settle at $83.98 a barrel.

Humana shares rose 3% after TD Cowen upgraded the healthcare services tech giant to buy from hold, raising the price target to $485, implying a 28% upside from the stock's Thursday close of $380.

"Taking into account 2026 performance, 2027 Medicare Advantage benefit design and 2028 Stars results, we see a relatively clear path towards a meaningful step-up in 2027 EPS growth and more than $40 EPS in 2028," the bank remarked in its note.

Adjusted EPS estimates for 2026, 2027, and 2028 remain unchanged at $9.51, $18.41, and $40.42, respectively.

Anthropic was the most-traded single stock by Vanguard's self-directed retail traders on Thursday, underscoring the buzz among mom-and-pop investors around the artificial intelligence leader's historic IPO.

Just about 0.2% of Vanguard's self-directed investors bought Anthropic on Thursday, which was its first day on the public market. These investors bought a median of 20 shares or roughly $1,950.

Vanguard noted about around out of every 10 Anthropic buyers were men. By comparison, men account for 55% of Vanguard's investor base.

To be sure, Vanguard said a higher percentage of its base traded SpaceX during its public market debut session in June.

Anthropic jumped 17% in trading on Thursday after it went public. But the stock has dropped nearly 10% in afternoon trading Friday, which is its first full day on the market.

BTIG's chief market technician Jonathan Krinsky in an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" Friday pointed to technicals that make him think the sell-off isn't over just yet.

He specifically noted Apple, the largest stock by market cap, which is only down by 3% from its 2026 highs earlier this month. "When the S&P has been down at least 8% or more, when it's made its final bottom, the median drawdown for Apple has been 23%," he noted. "It would be historically unprecedented to see a final bottom on the S&P with Apple where it is right now.".

He added that 50% of the S&P 500's stocks are above their 50-day moving average, a level that is higher than a number closer to below 40% — or even 20% — when durable bottoms hit.

Recent findings suggest that krinsky did note, though, that relief for semiconductors may be coming, as the group is retreating to levels that it last traded at in early April when the group started to surge higher. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) in late trading Friday was at levels it last closed below on April 9.

Anthropic debuted with a 17% advance on Thursday, starting off on the wrong foot as its performance came up short when compared with the day-one gains from other notable IPOs since last year.

The day-one moves of Circle, Figma, Cerebras and SpaceX all outdid Anthropic's, with Figma seeing the biggest jump at 250%.

Anthropic shares gave back much of that advance on Friday, falling more than 12% in afternoon trading.

President Donald Trump remarked on Friday that he wants to stop U.S. companies from building data centers in other countries.

"We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump mentioned at a White House press conference. He added that companies would face tremendous penalties for building data centers abroad. "We want them to build it here.".

Recent findings suggest that he added that he is concerned about U.S. companies building in China instead. "We're not allowing that to happen," he said.

— Kevin Breuninger and Davis Giangiulio.

The VIX volatility index, a gauge of how much the S&P 500 might move in the next 30 days based on options trading, rose another 13% intraday Friday to 32.27, after jumping as much as 16% Thursday, according to FactSet data.

According to recent reports, the VIX, a gauge of skittishness on Wall Street, has now risen for six of the past seven days. The index hasn't closed above 30 since late March.

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook expressed caution about the dangers posed by inflation, saying Friday that if the central bank doesn't act now it risks having to do more later.

"Inflation has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward," Cook noted in remarks delivered in Chile.

"Furthermore, waiting longer to implement rate increases risks getting behind the curve," she added. "If we fall behind, additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up, which could increase stress on our financial system and have unnecessarily damaging effects on American households.".

Cook was one of only two FOMC members who voted against the pause. Markets strongly expect the committee to approve a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.

Recent findings suggest that the tech selling intensified in late-morning trading, with the sector down more than 5% on the day. That decline pushed its week-to-date losses to 10.5% as of 11:57 a.m. ET. That would be tech's biggest one-week drop since April 4, 2025, when the Trump administration announced massive tariffs on imported products.

According to recent reports, the Nasdaq Composite dropped Friday, turning negative for 2026, as even Anthropic's IPO and Nvidia's earnings failed to revive the artificial intelligence trade. The tech-heavy index was last lower by 2.6% for the trading session, falling slightly on the year.

Bitcoin slid more than 4% with the broader market, falling below the $60,000 level for the first time since July.

The flagship cryptocurrency was last trading at $59,554.95 and is now heading for a retest its July low of $57,737.35.

Ether fell 6% to $1,650.79, its lowest level since July 2.

The outlook for consumers improved in November as expectations for inflation eased, according to a University of Michigan survey Friday.

The survey's headline sentiment index rose to 51.5, up 7.3% from a month ago and exactly in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate.

In a recent development, inflation expectations at the one-year horizon declined sharply, down to 3.7%, which was a full percentage point below a month ago and well below the mid-month November reading of 4.3%. This was the lowest reading since March. The five-year outlook slipped to 3.3%.

"Despite the softening in inflation expectations, consumers continue to report overwhelmingly that inflation—rather than unemployment—will cause greater hardship for consumers in the next one or two years," survey director Joanne Hsu noted.

The recent pressure seen in technology stocks as well as the S&P 500 may not be over yet, according to James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics.

"The success of Anthropic's IPO yesterday as other AI-related stocks tumbled highlights how different parts of the AI ecosystem no longer move as one," he wrote in a Friday note. "We think the falls in tech stocks and the S&P 500 have further to run — and how this plays out within the stock market will depend on what is driving these falls.".

Industry observers note that reilly believes the S&P 500 index should fall to 6,500 by the end of next year. The index closed at 7,175.83 on Thursday.

The three major averages were trading in the red on Friday morning.

The Nasdaq Composite declined 1.3% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the S&P 500 moved down 0.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 48 points, or 0.1%.

Anthropic made its historic Wall Street debut on Thursday. But one research firm is taken a cautious stance on the stock.

Seaport Research initiated coverage of the artificial intelligence stock with a neutral rating.

"Anthropic is an incredible company, but it is also asking for an incredible leap of faith by investors," analyst Jay Goldberg said in a note. "We think the company will need time to grow into its valuation and answer some very substantial questions about its growth trajectory. We are not negative on the company, but we are cautious.".

Check out CNBC's live blog here to read more about the stocks making premarket moves.

— Deena Zaidi, Darla Mercado and Fred Imbert.

Industry observers note that the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) was trading above 30 on Friday morning as the selling pressure on U.S. equity futures ramped up.

The index, also known as Wall Street's "fear gauge," was last at 30.99, reaching its highest level since March.

Shares of French video game publisher Ubisoft fell 13.2% in European morning trade, after the maker of the "Assassin's Creed" franchise forecast net bookings of around 250 million euros ($274 million) for the October to December period.

That was below a 361 million euro consensus estimate cited by analysts at TD Cowen and represents a fall from 338 million euros in the same quarter last year, at a time when hype in the market is being dominated by the launch of Take-Two's "Grand Theft Auto VI". Ubisoft cited a "particularly crowded holiday season" in its outlook.

Ubisoft on Thursday also reported net bookings down 16.5% year-on-year in its fiscal first half, with second-quarter net bookings of 389 million euros, above its guidance of around 370 million euros.

U.S. Treasury yields fell on Friday, as an equities sell-off drove investors into safe-haven assets ahead of Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller's speech later in the session.

The 10-year Treasury yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, loans and credit card debt — was down 6 basis points at 4.989%.

Industry observers note that the 2-year Treasury note yield, more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was also 6 basis points lower at 4.713%. The 30-year Treasury bond yield – which moves on wider geopolitical developments – was down 4 basis points at 5.361%.

Industry observers note that premarket moves point to continued downward momentum in Massive Tech, including Anthropic, which is seen 6% lower at 4:25 a.m. ET after its blockbuster debut.

Sources indicate that nvidia slipped 1.9% in premarket with the stock at its lowest level in more than a year following a rollercoaster period. Among other Mag 7 stocks, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon and Tesla dipped into the red, while Apple nudged 0.5% higher.

Semiconductor stocks fell, with Broadcom down 3%, AMD losing 4.95% and Micron shedding 3.8%.

According to recent reports, european chip players ASML and ASM International dropped 5.8% and 5.4%, respectively. That came after Japanese semiconductor stocks tumbled during Friday trade, with Tokyo Electron closing 7.06% lower, Lasertec shedding 9.21% and Renesas Electronics losing 7.02%.

Bénédicte Lowe, equity derivatives strategist at BNP Paribas, told CNBC there was a "mind-boggling" disconnect in the fact that a market sell-off has coincided with the biggest-ever IPO in Anthropic — but that investors were "panic selling" as they try to gauge whether AI sentiment has peaked.

Sources indicate that the sell-off is now in a second leg in which investors are even ditching traditionally defensive plays in a broad risk-off environment, she said. Tech worries are seeping into sectors such as FTSE 100 mining companies, hit by fears of a recession.

"No market can weather a proper unwind of the tech trade," Lowe said.

Any upside going into year-end will require a stabilization of the tech story and market moves, she added.

Matthias Reschke, head of European Investment Grade Finance for JP Morgan, told "Squawk Box Europe" that corporate spreads are looking "very resilient" in the wake of the equity market sell-off, though the market is "much more nervous than it used to be.".

With risk appetite down across markets and spreads widening, even for investment-grade corporates, he remarked this is where he expects "everyone is going to park their money.".

The big question is if inflation will come down next year, he added. Reschke expects persistent inflation pressures, meaning government 10-year yields may "remain elevated for a while.".

European stocks fell at Friday's open, with the benchmark Stoxx 600 index down 0.83% after hitting a four week-low on Thursday.

The region's technology stocks joined the global sell-off, last down 2.7%, with chip stocks ASML, ASM International and Be Semiconductor among the worst performers.

The market is skeptical about "all layers of the AI layer cake" but that can be a "great setup for investors," Brett Winton, chief futurist at ARK Investment Management who has Anthropic in all his portfolios, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday.

A key worry is that the huge R&D spend of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX will generate sufficient returns, he remarked.

"The market really thinks that Anthropic's revenue per gigawatt of compute has essentially peaked and is only going to go down from here. And the history and the returns they've got to their training suggest exactly the opposite, where they already have amazing gross margins," he remarked.

"What they're getting is the ability to serve more intelligence per GPU [graphics processing unit] that they use, and as they deliver on that, they're able to monetize per gigawatt of GPU more successfully... That's why you've seen Anthropic's growth margins expand as rapidly as they have, even as their top line has been explosively growing. So we think that's going to continue.".

On concerns about the infrastructure buildout around AI, Winton said people increasingly doubted whether companies will be willing to pay for the compute they're delivering to market.

"We take exactly the opposite view. So the overall market for knowledge workers we think is a $40 trillion market for AI software selling into the knowledge workforce, and so there's plenty of room to run if collectively Anthropic and OpenAI are only annualizing revenue on the order of $150 billion per year right now.".

"So we're really in the earliest, earliest stages of what will be a really dynamic game, and we think there's a lot of upside from here.".

Shares in Japan's SoftBank Group closed 14.48% lower on Friday, their worst day since August 2024, as a broader sell-off swept through Asian technology stocks.

The decline highlights investor concerns over SoftBank's aggressive bets on artificial intelligence, particularly its exposure to OpenAI, as markets question whether massive investments in AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns.

Industry observers note that the group is one of the biggest backers of OpenAI, Anthropic's rival. Read more.

Asia-Pacific markets ended sharply lower on Friday as a sweeping sell-off in technology stocks dragged major indexes across the region into negative territory.

Japan's Nikkei 225 plunged 5.06% to close at 56,436.65, while the Topix dropped 3.88% to 3,674.22.

South Korea's Kospi sank 5.21% to close at 4,869.96, while the small-cap Kosdaq shed 5.71% to 645.68.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 closed at 8,592.6.

Mainland China's CSI 300 slipped 0.76% to 3,954.57, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was down 2.24% in its final hour of trading.

British retail sales volumes rose by 0.7% in October, the country's Office for National Statistics mentioned Friday, continuing a choppy trend following a 0.6% decline in September and 0.8% gain in August.

The monthly figure was better than the flat reading forecast in a Reuters poll.

Recent findings suggest that retail activity was boosted over the summer by the soccer World Cup, while analysts expected weakening consumer sentiment and higher U.K. inflation to weigh on activity.

Traders continue to expect the Bank of England to hike interest rates by 25 basis points in December, though the odds of a hike have fallen to around 80% from 90% a week ago, according to money market pricing on LSEG.

Spot gold fell 2.81% to $3,520.05 per ounce on Friday, putting the precious metal on track for its worst weekly decline in eight months, according to Reuters.

Recent findings suggest that bullion, which hit its lowest since September 2025, has lost about 8.9% this week, according to LSEG data, pressured by a stronger U.S. dollar and growing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December.

Gold futures declined 4.55% to $3,519.20, a fresh 52-week low.

Taiwan's benchmark Taiex fell 5.65% on Friday, bringing its weekly losses to 14.89%, its steepest weekly decline since October 1997, according to LSEG data.

Recent findings suggest that taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the world's largest contract chipmaker and a key Nvidia supplier, dropped 4.52%. Other major Taiwanese technology stocks also fell, with Foxconn losing 4.08% and Wistron declining 4.49%.

The broader Asia tech stocks sold off on Friday, following declines in U.S. peers overnight.

Samsung Electronics announced a leadership reshuffle Friday, naming latest heads for its semiconductor and mobile businesses.

Sang Joon Hwang was promoted to president and named head of the memory business, while Sangyeun Cho was appointed president and will lead System LSI, which develops semiconductor chips including mobile processors and image sensors.

Jong Myeong Lee was promoted to president and named chief technology officer of the device solutions division, the organization said.

Industry observers note that samsung shares fell 6% amid a wider rout in Asian tech names, following a sell-off in U.S. AI stocks.

Shares of Chinese tech giant Alibaba rose 2.42%, bucking a broader sell-off in Asian markets, following robust earnings.

The gains followed Alibaba's quarterly earnings report on Thursday, which indicated operating income surging 443% from a year earlier to 29.12 billion yuan ($4.34 billion). Net income more than tripled to 64.42 billion yuan, helped by investment gains and improved operating performance.

Recent findings suggest that alibaba's gain stood out against a broader regional sell-off, with Japanese and South Korean technology shares sharply following overnight losses on Wall Street. Hong Kong's benchmark Hang Seng Index also dropped 2%.

Shares of Japan's SoftBank Group plunged 16.16% on Friday, leading a broader decline in Asian technology stocks following Anthropic's much-anticipated Wall Street debut.

SoftBank's substantial investment in Anthropic rival OpenAI has left it particularly exposed to shifts in AI investor sentiment.

Japanese chip stocks also fell sharply, with Tokyo Electron down 7.19%, Lasertec losing 6.75% and Renesas Electronics dropping 6.71%.

The sell-off extended to South Korea, where SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics declined 6% and 4.7%, respectively.

The decline in Asian tech names follows a slide overnight in U.S. stocks, with the Nasdaq Composite dropping more than 2%.

Japan's Nikkei 225 plunged 4.5% after data released Friday highlighted core inflation jumping to the highest this year at 2.2%, raising expectations of another rate hike in December.

The probability of a hike next month now stands at 72%, according to LSEG data.

The index was pressured by sharp declines in tech and related names, with SoftBank Group dropping 16%, chip-testing equipment maker Advantest plunging over 9% , while Tokyo Electron slid 7%.

Core inflation in Japan soared to a fresh high in 2026, coming in at 2.2% in October as higher energy costs and their knock-on effects pushed up prices in the wider economy.

Core inflation, which strips out prices of food, was lower than the 2.3% expected by Reuters-polled economists, but was higher than the 2.1% in prior month.

Energy subsidies for households expired in September, exposing consumers to higher prices brought about by the Iran war. Energy prices climbed 2.2% in October, a sharp spike from the 0.6% decline in September. Gas prices jumped 5.8% compared to the 2.4% rise the month before.

Asia-Pacific markets opened lower Friday, with South Korea's Kospi leading losses in the region.

Kospi fell 3.91% with tech heavy weights SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics down 6% and 4% respectively, and the small-cap Kosdaq declined 3.54% in early trading.

According to recent reports, japan's Nikkei 225 fell 1.46%, while the Topix was down 1.29%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 1.30%.

Asia-Pacific markets were set to open lower on Friday, tracking losses on Wall Street as Anthropic's highly anticipated stock market debut failed to boost investor sentiment around the broader AI names.

Futures for Japan's Nikkei 225 in Chicago were at 57,890 while in Osaka they were last at 57,880, compared with the index's previous close of 59,444.21.

Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index last traded at 22,759 compared with the index's last close of 22,841.62.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 1.02% in early trade.

California attorney general Rob Bonta sent an investigative subpoena to Nvidia, looking into whether the company's advanced chips may have gone to China.

"My office is investigating whether Nvidia or [former CEO] Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information – and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law," Bonta mentioned in a statement.

Shares were last down 0.2% in extended trading. Earlier in the day, Nvidia slid to a new 52-week low.

Read more from CNBC's Dan Mangan on the subpoena against Nvidia here.

The reason for the juxtaposition between Anthropic's strong IPO showing versus the market's sell-off Thursday is investor worries over two headwinds, according to Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer, Walser Wealth Management:.

The potential of slowing down with the Democratic wave in the recent midterm elections, combined with the scandal brought on by Jensen Huang stepping away as Nvidia CEO.

"If we are systemically facing headwinds that are going to slow down the AI data center development, they're going to be quite a bit of unwinding in valuations," Walser explained, adding that it will take a while for that uncertainty to "reverberate through all of the companies that have had positive upside because of the big AI capex.".

Still, Anthropic's record IPO is "a really substantial tell that the future of AI is secure, but we are facing headwinds, and we are going to have the volatility of the pullback from those headwinds," Walser added.

It has been revealed that dow Jones Industrial Average futures rose 9 points. S&P 500 futures slipped 0.1%, and Nasdaq-100 futures shed 0.2%.

This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos.
  • In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity.
  • To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first revealed. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

According to recent reports, the simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you stated) to your “Notes to self” note.

To take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.).

Sources indicate that all the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

It has been revealed that it’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.).

There’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can plan them better next time.

You’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

Sources indicate that but this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.).

The Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

Sources indicate that I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I remarked it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

Breaking: Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple, TTP respond]

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps.
  • Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable owners to generate nonconsensual nude images.
  • According to the updated rules, apps that allow people to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable owners to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow people to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow customers to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed users to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”.

In a recent development, A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of New Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta mentioned they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

According to recent reports, update, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple mentioned:.

Industry observers note that “We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for people. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”.

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The company added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the tech giant said does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

As for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Sources indicate that apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The company remarked that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

According to recent reports, upgrade, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:.

Apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps important concerns and leaves out key context. The organization indicates it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

Recent findings suggest that there are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The company defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also says it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

Recent findings suggest that as for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out new child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.

Recent findings suggest that FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses.
  • According to recent reports, that might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code.
  • Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all owners, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something newly introduced. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

According to recent reports, that might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all owners, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app. You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

To make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

In a recent development, with a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but indicates you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection.".

According to recent reports, the finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a upcoming window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

According to recent reports, I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

Industry observers note that for something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

According to recent reports, maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a major family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a latest website.

Industry observers note that bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

It looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

  • Sources indicate that the Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia's worst week on record just got worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books.

Industry observers note that nvidia (NVDA) stock fell nearly 14% Friday, its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss. The drop came as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting problems.

Sources indicate that the Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment.

According to recent reports, the selling set records. Nvidia shed about $485 billion in market value Friday and nearly $900 billion this week, as its stock had its worst week since October 2008. That tops the $573 billion it lost last week, previously the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet (GOOGL).

It has been revealed that nvidia's latest quarterly report raised a few questions. The organization mentioned its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.

According to recent reports, nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal stated the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China.

Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on.

Sources indicate that washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent remarked Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.

The sell-off spread across chip stocks, which had their worst week since 2001, and the broader market.

Baird's Ted Mortonson, a technology desk sector strategist, saw more scrutiny coming even before Friday's report.

"Every single deal that Nvidia has done on circular finance is going to be put under the microscope," he said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.

Every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an update that addresses one of its people’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

As spotted by The Verge, Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed today that the app will finally let customers edit a Story after publishing.

This means users will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

The catch is that owners will only have 15 minutes after publishing a Story to make changes by tapping the ellipsis button at the bottom of the screen, and then selecting “Edit story.”.

Here’s Mosseri’s post announcing the news:.

A post shared by Adam Mosseri (@mosseri).

Today’s enhancement is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

Recent findings suggest that back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting customers manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other demonstrates dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

According to recent reports, juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

In a recent development, A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Sources indicate that mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that quickly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

According to recent reports, peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The new Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a upcoming interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue noted Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:.

We were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:.

Sources indicate that when we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a big way on upcoming and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:.

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are newly introduced or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe mentioned “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very notable to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a new logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe noted he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:.

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The glitch of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:.

Industry observers note that well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a manufacturer and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift….

In a recent development, black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying.
  • Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.
  • The survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yellowjackets is a vibe. The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying. The dual timelines build tension around the story’s many mysteries, and the complex characters (no one’s completely good or evil on this show) make for a lot of surprising plot swerves that feel grounded despite the supernatural implications all around them. If you’re looking for more of that specific flavor of horror, you should probably watch Alive.

Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.

The survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances. They use the wrecked plane as shelter in the withering cold, they scavenge for anything that could be useful, and they ration out the only food they have: Some chocolates and a case of wine. But an early mistake leaves them without any food at all, and slowly they come to the sickening realization that their best chance at survival is to treat the corpses of their friends and families scattered around the crash site as a food source.

There’s no supernatural aspect, but the story has a similar tone of desperation and despair as Yellowjackets. These are people determined to survive in an impossible situation, and they do things that no one outside of their shared experience could possibly understand. The real-life origins of the story add a sense of horror that more than matches the fictional “It” that haunts the girls of Yellowjackets; putting yourself into that very real experience makes it clear just how terrified everyone was. Rent Alive on Prime Video.

If you’re craving more cannibals, cults, and crazies at the mercy of nature itself, here are a few more movies you should check out.

If you want to watch a movie that is essentially an adaptation of Yellowjackets, check out Eden. Even though it was released years before the show, the stories are so similar (albeit largely gender-flipped) that the producers of Eden actually sued, claiming plagiarism (they lost). In the film, a men’s soccer team (and two women on the same plane) crash-land on a deserted island, and as they fight for survival, things descend into, yes, madness and cannibalism as the survivors suffer dwindling food and water supplies and the rise of two violently opposed factions. It’s not nearly as deeply imagined as Yellowjackets, and it doesn’t have the supernatural hints of the show, but if you want a truly similar story, it’s a good choice. Stream Eden on The Roku Channel, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that you obviously cannot discuss Yellowjackets without discussing Lord of the Flies, William Golding’s 1954 novel about a group of schoolboys who descend into brutality and savagery when they’re stranded on a deserted island. The book has been adapted many times, but the 1963 version directed by Peter Brook is still the best version. Brook managed to elicit remarkably naturalistic performances from his young actors, giving the story a realistic tone that is somehow more terrifying than any amount of horror vibes. Stream Lord of the Flies on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that A slower and more haunting story, Picnic at Hanging Rock explores some of the same themes as Yellowjackets in an entirely different way. On Valentine’s Day in the year 1900, several students and teachers from an all-girls private school in Victoria, Australia, head to Hanging Rock for a picnic. Four students head off to explore and fall inexplicably asleep, and then three vanish, along with one of the teachers. Dreamy and drenched in dread, the story never offers any easy answers, and it explores themes of invading natural areas where you’re not wanted, burgeoning (and confusing) adolescent sexuality, and how our fear of the unknowable warps our perspective and often diminishes our humanity. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that you can never really go wrong with a Hitchcock film, and if you’re looking for another story about a disparate group of people forced to make terrifying decisions in order to survive, watch Lifeboat (based on a story by John Steinbeck). One of the director’s most underrated films, it’s the story of a group of survivors in a lifeboat after a German U-boat sinks their ship during World War II (including one survivor from the German boat). It’s a masterful suspense engine that’s not afraid to have its characters discuss the moral and ethical quandaries facing them as they struggle to survive and maintain their humanity under a constant threat of death. Stream Lifeboat on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

In a recent development, if you love the supernatural aspects of Yellowjackets as the girls come to believe a force they call “It” is out in the woods, check out The Ritual. Four friends embark on a hike in the wilds of northern Sweden to honor their deceased friend. When one of them is injured, they leave the marked trail to take a shortcut through the forest—where they are soon forced to shelter in an abandoned cabin, just like the Yellowjackets—and things begin to slide into the terrifying when they encounter a cult worshipping an ancient deity that grants them immortality in exchange for human sacrifices. It’s as if the show was condensed to an hour-and-a-half and the terror quotient was turned way, way up. Stream The Ritual on Netflix.

💡 Key Takeaways
