  • It has been revealed that so, if you’re heading to Leonida over the weekend, here are three major mistakes I've already made, and most importantly, how you can avoid doing the same stupid things as me (all spoiler-free).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto VI offers a size befitting the 13-year wait. Not only is the Vice City map absolutely huge, but it’s the most system-rich and mechanically deep game in the Grand Theft Auto series to date. There’s an overwhelming amount of things to see, do, and learn.

It has been revealed that like millions of gamers worldwide, I dived into the game at midnight, the very second it unlocked on my PS5 Pro. I’ve since put five hours of playtime into GTA 6, and while I’m still getting my head around all that the game has to offer (my completion percentage is a mere 12%), I’ve already learnt a few lessons the hard way. Yes, mistakes have been made.

It has been revealed that so, if you’re heading to Leonida over the weekend, here are three major mistakes I've already made, and most importantly, how you can avoid doing the same stupid things as me (all spoiler-free). Learn from my errors!

After 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived. Set in the state of Leonida, with Vice City at its heart, you play Jason and Lucia, two criminals forced into an increasingly dangerous situation as they seek their fortune, discovering the darker side of the sunniest spot in America.

It has been revealed that GTA 6 introduces a new money system in which you can hold cash either on your person or stashed securely at your safehouse. If you get “wasted” or “busted” by the cops, you’ll lose all the money you’re carrying, but the funds kept under the floorboards at Jason's beachside home are protected.

Recent findings suggest that as a cautious type, I took this to mean never carry any money on your person for fear of losing it, which pretty swiftly proved to be an oversteer when an early mission required me to buy a gun, and I literally had $0 in my wallet. This forced a trip back to the safehouse, where I counted out the exact number of bills required to buy the weapon.

Sources indicate that once I returned to the Ammu-nation store, I bought my gun and then was presented with a range of attachments (some with a limited-time discount), which I couldn’t buy because, again, I’d only brought the specific amount required to buy the gun itself. Frustrating.

This taught me not to fear actually carrying money in your wallet. Sure, running about Vice City with your entire bank balance on hand is probably unwise, but you’re going to want, and need, some money in your pocket. At this early stage, I’ve been opting for a 50/50 split, keeping half my ill-gotten gains in my stash, and the other half within instant reach.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

My approach to previous GTA games tended to be this: Complete a few story missions, and then go on a psychotic rampage to blow off some steam (I swear I’m not a total psycho).

Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 is different. For pretty much the first time in the franchise’s history, the game actively discourages you from causing carnage without purpose through the newly introduced “Criminal Profile” system. Your in-game actions are tracked and contribute to the type of criminal Jason (and later Lucia) is becoming. Ranging from a “professional” all the way to a full-blown “psycho.”.

During my first GTA 6 session, after completing the mandatory prologue, I decided to see how many wanted stars I could rack up with just the starter pistol, and pretty quickly the game warned me that my criminal spree would have consequences. It felt like that old Tellale’s The Walking Dead warning message, “Clementine will remember that…”.

Rockstar has confirmed your “Criminal Profile” will impact how the story plays out, and I certainly don’t want to receive a “bad” ending; such was my concern about how my early game rampage would impact how my GTA 6 story plays out, I opted to reload to a previous save to instantly wash away the worrying amount of blood already on Jason’s hands.

So, in GTA 6, it pays to show restraint. You will commit many crimes, of course, but resist the urge to go full GTA and instead commit your criminal acts with purpose and even planning.

Sources indicate that speaking of planning, from what I’ve played so far, GTA 6 is the most ambitious Grand Theft Auto yet in all areas, including mission design. Previous GTA games present players with cinematic but largely linear missions; if you tried to get creative, the game would promptly shepherd you back onto the golden path with instant fail states for any deviations.

Recent findings suggest that to be clear, GTA 6 does have these types of missions as well, but there’s a larger focus on player choice and letting you pick your approach. As an early (spoiler-free) example, a Chapter 1 mission asks you to retrieve a red sports car from a police impound lot.

Recent findings suggest that you’re dropped off right outside the main gate, with an on-screen prompt encouraging you to break the lock. Naturally, I obliged, and the impound’s alarms started blaring; every cop in the area was instantly alerted, and the mission pretty much went further south from there.

It has been revealed that one reload later, I was back at the mission start, and this time, I slowed down. I cased the joint first, walking the perimeter, trying to find a subtler way to access the impound lot. And what do you know, a conveniently placed scissor lift around the corner got me onto the roof, allowing me to quietly drop into the compound without setting off any alarms or alert cops.

It’s a reminder that in GTA 6, thinking before you act can pay off, and when you factor in the “Criminal Profile” system, there is real merit in completing missions without having to shoot your way out of trouble.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The open-source Devin alternative: a coding agent your team works with in Slack, on its own computers, in your cloud or ours.

Cloud | Self-hosting | Docs | Website | Benchmark | Community | X.

Recent findings suggest that openComputer is the open source, self hostable alternative to Devin. Mention @Computer in a Slack thread with a task, it works on its own computer, you & your team can watch and steer it as it goes, and the result lands as a pull request.

It is open source from the compute layer up, so you can run all of it in your own cloud account, or start on OpenComputer Cloud in two minutes.

We built it to feel as fast as Claude Code on your laptop: in our benchmark it opens PRs 3.3x faster than Devin.

OpenComputer is built to be simple to self-host without giving up scale or security. The whole stack runs on a single VM, which we recommend locking down to outbound-only network access.

According to recent reports, the VM runs the gateway, Calvin: a thin bridge that listens for Slack events and starts a session with Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode, depending on your configuration. Each session is isolated with rootless Podman. Its state is written first to the VM's local disk, then persisted to a git-backed store.

In a recent development, the rest of the stack runs on Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects. Support for Fly and other platforms is coming soon.

Breaking: Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • Sources indicate that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • Industry observers note that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

Sources indicate that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

Industry observers note that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

It has been revealed that A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

Sources indicate that “It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn promptly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

According to recent reports, miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

Sources indicate that during totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

In a recent development, druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly reveals Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs highlights the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

In a recent development, despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

Sources indicate that the corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

Industry observers note that that’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

In a recent development, space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very rapidly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she states, of solar eclipse photography.

Recent findings suggest that the European Proba-3 mission, introduced in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

According to recent reports, it took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

Sources indicate that the error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” notes Habbal.

Sources indicate that capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

In a recent development, the human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller indicates. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

It has been revealed that the teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

Sources indicate that but duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller states wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

According to recent reports, but even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” notes Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

In a recent development, twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

In a recent development, around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

Recent findings suggest that “Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as swiftly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller states. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

In a recent development, but for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Industry observers note that amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale has officially started—but keeping track of the best discounts yet to land and figuring out which deals are worthwhile can be a challenge. As an alternative, you can have Alexa give you a heads-up about deals on products you already know you want to purchase, so you don’t have to spend time sorting through the noise.

Then head to the Alexa mobile app and go to More in the top left (the three horizontal lines) > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping and toggle on Deal Recommendations under the Shopping Recommendations options. This ensures you’ll receive notifications for items that appear in your shopping activity.

It has been revealed that if Alexa finds an upcoming deal on something in your Saved for Later, your Wish List, or in your Shopping Cart, you’ll receive a pop-up alert on your Echo Show display or see a yellow light ring on your Echo speaker. You can also ask, “Alexa, what are my notifications?” to hear a list of deals it has compiled thus far. You can also say "Alexa, let me know when [product name] goes on sale.".

In a recent development, alexa can detect deals up to 24 hours in advance, so you can either ask it to remind you again when a deal starts or request that it buy the item when the deal goes live. Simply say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” and it’ll charge the default payment and send the item to the default delivery address on your account.

Latest Update: GTA 6’s 30 FPS lock broke my PC gamer brain — until I turned on the one TV setting I swore I’d never touch

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve ever bought a latest TV and invited a tech nerd like me into your living room, you already know I’m grabbing your remote, diving into the picture settings, and disabling motion smoothing.
  • Sources indicate that for movies and prestige TV, it is a crime against humanity — turning a cinematic masterpiece into an episode of "Days of Our Lives" shot on a camcorder.
  • And yet, here I am, playing Grand Theft Auto VI with motion smoothing cranked on, and refusing to turn it off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve ever bought a latest TV and invited a tech nerd like me into your living room, you already know I’m grabbing your remote, diving into the picture settings, and disabling motion smoothing.

Sources indicate that for movies and prestige TV, it is a crime against humanity — turning a cinematic masterpiece into an episode of "Days of Our Lives" shot on a camcorder. I hate it. Tom Cruise hates it. You should hate it too.

And yet, here I am, playing Grand Theft Auto VI with motion smoothing cranked on, and refusing to turn it off.

Sources indicate that to understand how I ended up committing TV heresy, you have to understand the shock to the system that is GTA 6’s frame rate. Coming straight from my monster PC rig playing games like Resident Evil Requiem at up to 214 FPS, dropping back down to a strict 30 FPS console lock feels like wading through treacle.

Industry observers note that but on top of that, as I’ve seen (and you’ve seen on Digital Foundry’s test), that 30 FPS lock isn’t an actual lock. It can dip into the mid-20s during heavy scenes. Coming from super fluidity, that 30 FPS is brutal to adapt to.

So out of sheer desperation (and because we’re stuck waiting for the PC port), I broke the golden rule and toggled my TV’s smooth motion setting on.

And I hate to admit it, but it’s basically bootleg DLSS Frame Generation for your living room.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Just like PC frame generation tricks of old, your TV’s motion interpolation processor looks at two real frames from your console, guesses what should happen in between them, and inserts an artificial frame to smooth out the motion.

The moment I flipped it on in GTA 6, that nauseating camera stutter when cruising down Ocean Beach vanished. Panning around a crowded street or taking a high-speed corner suddenly felt dramatically more fluid — nowhere near 60 fps, and definitely not my desktop rig, but miles smoother than the choppy presentation.

Recent findings suggest that before the AV forums come for my head with pitchforks, let’s be completely honest about the trade-offs. There is no such thing as a free lunch in frame interpolation:.

Industry observers note that because your TV has to wait for the next frame before it can invent the one in the middle, motion smooth adds latency between pressing a button and seeing the result on screen. In twitchy, competitive games, that’s a death sentence.

But in a Rockstar open-world game — where character movement is already famously weighty and deliberate — I never noticed that extra latency.

Your TV’s processor is just guessing after all, and while it is a good guesser, there are some moments of weird shimmering around fast-moving objects and some boiling around on-screen elements like subtitles. Probably compounded by the fact GTA 6 is already running its own resolution scaling tech under the hood.

Standard Game Mode and VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) automatically lock out motion smoothing on many TVs. Depending on your set, you either have to turn on the dedicated low-latency Game Motion Plus mode (found on newer Samsung and LG sets) or sacrifice VRR to unlock it.

The silver lining, though, is that with this being a 30 FPS game, it’s not high enough to require VRR anyway.

If GTA 6’s 30 FPS cap is giving your eyes a workout and you want to test the dark arts yourself, don’t just blindly max out every slider.

If your TV has a low-latency interpolation option (like Samsung’s Game Motion Plus or LG’s TruMotion tweaks), use that before turning off Game Mode completely.

Set Judder Reduction to a middle ground (around 5-7 out of 10) rather than maxing it out. You want to take the harsh edge off camera pans without turning your car into a blurry smudge.

Sources indicate that this is optional based on personal taste. Test how your TV’s smoothing looks with GTA’s built-in motion blur turned off. For a lot of OLED owners, letting the TV handle the smoothing cleanly beats stacking two different blur effects on top of each other.

Do I want to play GTA 6 at native 240 FPS on my PC rig? Obviously. The second Rockstar drops the PC version, I’ll be uninstalling this hack from my brain and never looking back.

Industry observers note that I still wouldn’t be caught dead watching a movie with motion smoothing turned on. But until PC gamers get their turn in Vice City, breaking the ultimate TV rule is the best survival trick I’ve found for making a 30 FPS masterpiece actually feel better to play.

In a recent development, also yes, my wife has taken note of the fact that I share the same name as the male protagonist. And yes, she is side-eyeing how I treat Lucia hard.

The best Black Friday phone deals can save you hundreds of dollars on a brand newly introduced handset, but they're not the only deals available right now. There are plenty of phone accessories that are being discounted too, but choosing between them can be quite tricky.

Recent findings suggest that lucky for you, I've spent a lot of time using different phone accessories, and know how to spot a good deal when they appear. I've already spotted a bunch of deals on things I already own, but there are also a bunch of enticing deals for things I know I'm going to need — and I'm passing on the best ones to you.

Here are the seven best Black Friday phone accessory deals I'd buy right now.

In a recent development, screen protectors used to be the bane of my existence until they started selling kits for easy application. Now, the only time I mess up applying a screen protector is when I didn't clean the screen properly.

There are a lot of applicators out there, but I like this style from Tocol. Place the applicator on your phone before pulling the strip to expose the adhesive on the back of the screen protector. Press it down, and you can sit back and watch the air bubbles disappear.

Energizer is good for more than just batteries, and this wireless charging stand is crazy cheap for Black Friday. The 15W stand is capable of charging your phone, earbuds and an Apple Watch, with folding mechanisms that let it take up less space when you're not using it. Best Buy are also giving away three months of Apple Music and a month of Apple TV with every purchase.

In a recent development, remember when any charger faster than 10W used to be enormous? That's no longer the case, and Anker's 45W Nano charger is easily one of my favorite compact options. Not only is it small and portable, the metal prongs fold into the charging brick for even better portability. Plus there's a boost mode that allows up to 65W charging speeds for limited periods.

Anker also sells a 47W variant with two USB-C ports, which is presently on sale for $18 and a $25 version that features a mini screen displaying your recharge progress.

Recent findings suggest that energizer also sells a magnetic power bank, which clips onto the back of compatible phones with MagSafe and other compatible connectors. Speed is limited to 15W for wireless charging and 18W wired charging — if you even use it for that. A 5,000 mAh version is also available for $12, with a slightly thinner design.

According to recent reports, the Popsocket is the one phone accessory I wouldn't ever live without, and the MagSafe-compatible version is easily the most convenient. Not only does it give you a secure grip, which doubles as a phone stand, its easy to remove and replace.

That way you can swap it out for other MagSafe accessories when needed, or mix up the design whenever your mood strikes.

I know the pitfalls of not using a phone case all too well, and would encourage everyone to protect their phone with one. But which one do you buy? I've always been partial to Otterbox cases, on account of how much effort goes into protecting your phone.

In fact, my dad once claimed that an Otterbox kept his iPhone safe the time he foolishly decided to reverse his car over it. I don't know whether he was exaggerating or not, but it's stuck in my head ever since.

The downside is that Otterbox cases are expensive, but with $21 off that price feels a lot more reasonable.

One of the things I hate about travelling is not having all the comforts at home available. Which is especially awkward when it comes to charging my devices. Thankfully, Belkin's folding wireless charger folds up in a way that's well suited to travel.

Sources indicate that the Qi2.2 magnetic charger supports 25W wireless charging speeds, and includes a fold-out Apple Watch charger for extra convenience. It comes with built-in cooling, while also being bundled with a suitable 45W charging brick and USB-C cable, which doesn't always happen.

#16702. Signal Is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

Signal Is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1442 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Signal

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.
  • This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.
  • According to recent reports, we’ve already had to do this once with Windows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meredith Whittaker on 20 Nov 2026.

Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

According to recent reports, we’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default.1 We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen.2.

The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.

It has been revealed that in order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android.2.

It has been revealed that people who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.

In a recent development, we want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.3.

Sources indicate that we are also struggling with a significant lack of documentation about how these AI agents actually work. Over the past few months, we’ve spent considerable developer time and energy doing forensic investigations across Android and iOS in an attempt to learn what is actually happening when these AI systems access application data. Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.

In a recent development, we continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google, and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. In particular, we are calling on these companies to provide two common-sense remedies that can protect the privacy so many millions of people rely on:.

We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.

According to recent reports, in addition to taking these technical measures to block capture, we are engaging in conversations across the ecosystem to make the stakes clear. There is a lot of work to be done in the industry to improve the ways that AI agents operate in the operating system, and how and whether they capture and process private data. We are cautiously optimistic that some major OS providers, like Google and Apple, are engaging with us on how these systems should better interface with privacy-sensitive apps like Signal. We hope to have more to share on this topic soon, and that these companies recognize the danger to the ecosystem and work with us and others to create standardized approaches that meaningfully protect privacy across the industry.

According to recent reports, finally, we want to acknowledge that we are not the only ones recognizing these perils, and we are grateful to our allies for pushing for similar changes. We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data. Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.

Sources indicate that signal Technology Foundation is the nonprofit home of the Signal app, which is trusted by millions around the world. We protect free expression and enable secure global communication through open source privacy technology. Signal Technology Foundation is a US 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization.

Sources indicate that microsoft Recall captures your screen every few seconds, extracts text from screenshots via optical character recognition, then populates a searchable on-device database with this personal data in order to allow the AI system to query it – potentially exposing and retaining your Signal data indefinitely, including disappearing messages. ↩.

There are multiple versions of Android beyond the Google-provided distributions on Pixel devices. For many vendors, we don’t have a reliable way to detect when a screenshot was attempted if screenshots are already disabled. Rather than choose a poor user experience (where screenshots simply stop working, confusing customers), we decided to instead focus on detecting when an AI assistant attempts to access the screen. We automatically enable the “Screen security” setting in Signal Android when this type of access is detected. ↩ ↩2.

Careful readers will note that in addition to not being able to cover all Android devices, we are also not blocking Siri AI on macOS. This is because we cannot reliably block screenshots on macOS. Faced with a lack of clearly documented APIs that allow us to implement screenshot protection, we do not have the tools available that let us do the job. While protections against continuous screen capture exist on macOS, we cannot apply them to screenshots (which is how most agentic systems access data from applications like Signal). Trying to implement screenshot blocking on macOS has revealed to us a minefield of bewildering decisions that place user privacy at risk, including APIs that have been deprecated in favor of screen-protection solutions that only work for streaming media and other DRM-protected content. This is something we hope Apple remedies urgently. For now, the only recommendation we have for macOS 27 consumers is to add Signal to the Excluded Apps section in System Settings > Siri to protect message content from proactive access by Siri AI. ↩.

Industry observers note that if you’re going to commit to an Amazon Prime membership, you might as well squeeze as much as you can out of the deal. And there's a good amount of juice to squeeze there. The price you pay for Amazon depends on many factors, but regardless of how much you're paying, it's worth it for most people (we've done the math).

If you're on the fence about signing up, consider that Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is underway, and the firm is hosting some amazing tech deals. It's a great time to sell your soul—or take advantage of the 30-day free trial—and there's a lot more to your membership than just deals and free shipping.

Recent findings suggest that the standard Prime membership costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, but there are other tiers that some people might qualify for. For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):.

Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

According to recent reports, amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

In a recent development, A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

Sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. This grants access to all the standard benefits, such as free delivery, Prime Video with ads, Prime Reading, third-party benefits like Grubhub, and access to audiobooks, e-books, certain games, and Amazon Music.

Amazon Health: Prime customers get One Medical access for an additional $9 per month or $99 per year. Through your devices, you’ll have 24/7 access to on-demand virtual care, plus real-life access to primary care offices in a number of U.S. cities. It accepts most major health insurance intends, too.

Amazon Pharmacy: Access to free two-day delivery and other savings on medications.

Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV indicates, and Amazon Originals with ads, which normally costs $9 per month.

Amazon Music Prime: Access to Amazon's Spotify-esque music streaming service (not to be confused with Amazon's other music streaming subscriptions).

Amazon Luna: A cloud gaming platform that offers new free games every month, free downloadable PC games, content, a monthly Twitch channel subscription, and a free channel subscription on Twitch each month for Prime Members.

Amazon Photos: Unlimited photo storage plus 5 GBs for videos and other files (which extends to members of your Family Vault).

Prime Reading: Free access to a rotating selection of e-books and magazines for Kindle or Fire tablets and Kindle apps.

Amazon's First Reads: You get up to two free e-books every month from a curated list of books handpicked by editors.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user ….
  • Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was introduced the same month, with the manufacturer describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta employees have expressed concerns about what appear to be major privacy breaches when using Muse, currently the second most popular free iPhone app in the App Store with over 10 million downloads.

This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user ….

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was introduced the same month, with the manufacturer describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”.

Recent findings suggest that muse initially launched as an iPhone app, with Mac and iPad apps following shortly afterwards. It immediately moved to the top of the US App Store charts, overtaking ChatGPT. It quickly exceeded 5 million downloads following a major advertising push by Meta, and that number has since doubled.

Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t long before major privacy concerns were raised. Tech writer Jason Aten reported that the Mac app accessed his messages despite him explicitly refusing permission. The app then lied to him about how it had achieved this. Meta described this as a bug.

Security researcher Patrick Wardle also discovered a zero-day vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack dictated prompts, directing them instead to their own server.

I stated at the time that I would absolutely not be one of the millions of people using the app, and the wisdom of that decision has now been underlined by a fresh report.

Industry observers note that reuters now reports Meta employees discussing further breaches. This includes another example of accessing encrypted messages without permission.

An employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp.

“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee remarked in her post.

Recent findings suggest that the report states this appears to have been done by capturing push notifications. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. The AI Now Institute was able to replicate the problem of Muse accessing Signal messages without permission.

Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user.

Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”.

“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

According to recent reports, meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information. Patch: Meta has now told us that the balances were definitely hallucinations.

"AI Agent" = Malware. There are an expanding number of "I told it not to do that" cases.

Industry observers note that the instructions (prompt) you give the agent are a tiny fraction of the total prompt context the agent uses, and Meta/Grok/etc. is not going to let you see that context. Agents harvesting your data (ex. see full disk access) and sending it to the mothership is just another revenue/training stream. Even if you are paying you are still the product.

Meta has taken matter with the messaging claims. It says that access to either notifications or messaging must be explicitly granted.

Sources indicate that with Android, users have the option to grant apps notification access, which allows apps to see notifications as they’re received. This is something users need to opt in to and is not specific to Muse. With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on.

The organization also implies that the experience of employees may relate to internal versions of Muse.

Employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.

I can only repeat my previous take on Muse: Nope.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's official, and there's no escaping it — Black Friday is here. With it comes huge discounts on everything from Ninja appliances to Dyson vacuums to MacBooks and iPhones — and soundbars.

Upgrading your home cinema setup has never been cheaper (well, except maybe in like 2001 or something). Amazon has reduced the price of all its own-brand soundbars, including the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar for just $74, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus for $139, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar with Subwoofer for $229, and the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar with Subwoofer and Rears for $349.

I've reviewed both the $74 2.0-channel soundbar and the $139 3.1-channel soundbar with built-in subwoofer, and both really surprised me, especially the $74 model. This is by far the cheapest soundbar I've ever awarded a 4.5-star rating — I would snap this one up for an instant TV speaker upgrade.

The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is the cheapest option on Amazon's home theater lineup, but it's the most surprising. With powerful bass and a fantastic dialogue mode, I didn't miss a thing during testing.

Sources indicate that the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus is extremely well-priced at its MSRP of $249, but $139 is almost incomprehensibly cheap. While the subwoofer can be a little boomy, if you mostly watch Netflix and YouTube, this won't be an matter at all.

Industry observers note that the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer is an excellent level up. If you value clear and controlled bass, this would be the option for you. This model has clearer dialogue than the built-in subwoofer version.

For those who value true surround sound, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer and Rears is your best bet. This is the only model capable of true Dolby Atmos, so movie fanatics need look no further.

Breaking: Canva introduces latest controls to hide generative AI features

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In light of growing pushback from users who want more control over how AI is integrated into their apps (if at all), Canva is introducing fresh settings that let them hide generative AI features and see less AI-generated content.
  • Canva today revealed newly introduced controls that will let Free and Pro users choose whether to see generative AI features across the app, as well as how much AI-generated content appears in search results and in recommendations for templates and design elements.
  • The firm notes that both controls are available at no additional cost and can be turned on or off at any time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In light of growing pushback from users who want more control over how AI is integrated into their apps (if at all), Canva is introducing fresh settings that let them hide generative AI features and see less AI-generated content. Here are the details.

Canva today revealed newly introduced controls that will let Free and Pro users choose whether to see generative AI features across the app, as well as how much AI-generated content appears in search results and in recommendations for templates and design elements.

The firm notes that both controls are available at no additional cost and can be turned on or off at any time.

According to Canva, “the future of creativity isn’t a choice between AI and no AI.” For this reason, it is introducing the following controls:.

The organization says that, while it knows that there is an ongoing debate between users with opposing views on whether AI has a place in creative work, it thinks “both views are valid”:.

“It’s not our place to tell anyone how to create, so today we’re launching two new controls that put that decision firmly with our community […].”.

Importantly, the company noted that select features that use AI without generating new content will remain available even when generative AI features are turned off:.

“Some of Canva’s everyday editing tools use AI to make simple tasks faster, without generating anything fresh. Background Remover, one of Canva’s most popular tools, lifts a subject cleanly out of a photo in a single click, and Magic Grab lets creators select an object in an image and move it somewhere else in the design. Both remain available when the generative AI switch is off, because they work only with what’s already in a design.”.

Canva added that these tools also won’t add an AI label to a design’s metadata, since that label is reserved for AI-generated content.

As for the company’s design content library, Canva noted that while “a small portion of the library is AI-generated content made by Canva, including some abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics,” its community has told it “they want an easier way to find design assets made by real people, so the content control reduces the number of AI-generated templates and elements that appear in search results and recommendations.”.

With today’s announcement, Canva is essentially expanding on the AI permissions already available to administrators of Business, Enterprise, Teams, and Education accounts, which let organizations control how their teams use AI.

#16696. Frostbite: A fresh CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2929 w)
