Industry observers note that micro coils are the newest innovation for toppers so they’re often priced higher than expected. Considering the pricing of Saatva’s other mattress toppers, $315 for a queen Micro-Coil Mattress Topper seems about right for the brand. The topper is shipped for free and comes with a six-month sleep trial and one-year warrantym which is considered pretty a short warranty period for the luxury topper market.

According to recent reports, the Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper has three different layers. The top layer is a cotton cover with Guardin botanical antimicrobial treatment. It prevents the growth of bacteria, mildew, and mold, which is helpful considering the cover is not removeable (and thus not washable).

Sources indicate that in the centre of the mattress topper is a one-inch layer of recycled steel micro-coils. They’ve been reinforced along the edges of the topper and in the center third to provide support for your hips and lower back. On either side of the micro-coil layer is gel-infused comfort foam with CertiPUR-US certification for enhanced temperature control.

Four straps are placed on the corners to keep the topper in place. Though I ordered a king topper, it did not fully cover my king-sized mattress, exposing about an inch or two on either side of the topper. (This has been the case for all of the Saatva toppers I've tested, which makes me wonder if my actual mattress is larger than I thought).

According to recent reports, my biggest concern about this mattress’ design might be the durability. Foam breaks down faster than natural latex and there is only an inch between your body and the micro coil layer. While I didn’t notice any durability problems during testing, the plusher, soft surface of the topper indicates a softer foam that may not last as long as a firmer foam, especially if you sleep in the same spot night after night.

After a week of testing the Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper, here’s what I can share about the ease of set up, comfort, and temperature regulation.

The Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper arrived vacuum sealed and tightly rolled into a ball. Because of the micro-coils, I had to unfurl the topper by hand and place it in a flat position on my mattress. After putting the straps into place so the topper wouldn’t move, I noticed that it didn’t completely cover my king-size mattress. There was about an inch or two of the mattress visible on either side of the topper.

The topper had a lot of creases and bunching because it appears to have unnecessary, extra fabric. By the time I slept on the topper at night, I could not feel the fabric through my sheets.

The off-gassing of the topper’s foams were noticeable as soon as I removed the packaging, and a week later, I can still smell it.

For a mattress topper with a layer of micro coils, I expected it to be firm and supportive. That’s how Saatva advertises it, but that’s not exactly what I experienced.

According to recent reports, the Micro-Coil Mattress Topper has a plush, soft surface — I rate it as 5/10 on the mattress firmness scale, placing it as medium-plush. My shoulders and hips sunk in enough to allow for deep pressure relief when on my side and felt comfortably supportive when on my back. As a back and stomach sleeper who prefers a firmer mattress feel, the topper was slightly too soft for my preferences. However, the cushioning and cradling nature of the surface would appeal to most sleepers.

Stomach sleepers will need something firmer, like the Saatva Graphite Mattress Topper, especially those weighing over 180lbs. Comfort-wise, I’d recommend the Micro-Coil Mattress Topper to those who need to soften a firm mattress.

Thanks largely to its recycled steel coils, the Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper does a decent job with temperature regulation. However, I wouldn’t suggest it for very hot sleepers.

It has been revealed that I tested this topper during a particularly cold week in Texas in November when the temperature inside my home was between 64-69 degrees at night. Because it was so cold in the evenings, I’d sometimes fall asleep with a sweatshirt and sweatpants. When that happened, I would wake up slightly warm — but not sweating and not hot. I’d then take off my socks or change into lighter pyjamas and be fine the rest of the night.

The best mattress toppers will provide a comfortable sleep feel, regardless of the temperature of your bedroom. If you like the sound of the Micro-coil, I’d suggest light sleepwear and using breathable sheets.

Whether you overheat easily or not, I’d suggest ordering this topper in the summer and utilize the 180-night sleep trial to make sure it’s a good fit for you.

In a recent development, rather than separate the topper reviews, Saatva mixed them all together. This means the 4.7 out of 5-star rating from over 305 reviews is a score related to all Saatva’s toppers – and is not accurate for the Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper.

In a recent development, you can search the topper reviews by keyword and star rating. I typed in “micro coil” and only six reviews popped up. There could be more by other buyers who didn’t mention the term “micro-coil” in their reviews.

Sources indicate that five of the six reviews praised the topper for its soft, contouring feel and how it improved their sleep by making their mattress more comfortable and/or its ability to relieve their pain. One reviewer mentioned returning the micro-coil mattress because it made them very hot at night.

✅You sleep on your side: Your shoulders and hips will sink in the right amount to allow for a comfortable night’s sleep on your side.

✅ You have a mattress that’s too firm: If your mattress is so firm that it’s causing you aches and pains, go for the Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper as it’ll provide the right amount of softening to your bed.

✅You have back or joint pain: The zoned lumbar support has been designed to support the spine and reduce pressure in the lumbar region.

In a recent development, ❌ You sleep on your stomach: Those who have smaller bodies (180-lbs. and below) could potentially sleep on your stomach on this mattress. However, for most, it won’t offer the firm support you’d need for a night of stomach sleeping.

In a recent development, ❌ You sleep very hot: The comfort foam layer feels a little stuffy, even with the inclusion of breathable steel coils. For very hot sleepers, I recommend the Saatva Natural Latex Topper instead, which is naturally cooling.

❌ You want a washable, removable cover: You can only spot clean the exterior of this topper as the cover can’t be removed and washed.

This copper-infused memory foam topper is cover free, and our reviewers found that it kept them cool at night. Its 7-zone surface technology has differing firmness levels along seven different areas of the body for superb zoned support. Read more in our Molecule CopperWELL Mattress Topper.

Sources indicate that enjoy a superbly cool night’s sleep on the Helix GlacioTex Premium Mattress Topper, a 3.75" thick topper that comes in two different firmness options. Like the Saatva Micro-Coil Mattress Topper, it has a layer of coils that aid in breathability. However, the GlacioTex cover probably does a better job to keep you from sweating or overheating at night.

In a recent development, if you love the Saatva brand and prefer something a bit more supportive, consider the Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper. It’s great for combination sleepers or couples with different sleep styles. The natural latex materials promote a cooler night’s sleep, especially for those who sleep hot. In the early 1960s, Richard Feynman gave a series of undergraduate lectures that were collected into a book called the Feynman Lectures on Physics. Absent from the book was a lecture Feynman gave on planetary motion, but a later finding of the notes enabled David Goodstein, a colleague of Feynman’s, to write a book about it: Feynman’s Lost Lecture. From an excerpt of the book published in a 1996 issue of Caltech’s Engineering & Science magazine:.

Industry observers note that feynman was a truly great teacher. He prided himself on being able to devise ways to explain even the most profound ideas to beginning students. Once, I remarked to him, “Dick, explain to me, so that I can understand it, why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics.” Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.”.

John Gruber writes the simple explanations are the goal at Apple as well:.

Engineers are expected to be able to explain a complex technology or product in simple, easily-understood terms not because the executive needs it explained simply to understand it, but as proof that the engineer understands it completely.

Feynman was well known for simple explanations of scientific concepts that result a in deeper understanding of the subject matter: e.g. see Feynman explaining how fire is stored sunshine, rubber bands, how trains go around curves, and magnets. Critically, he’s also not shy about admitting when he doesn’t understand something…or, alternately, when scientists as a group don’t understand something. There’s the spin anecdote above and of his explanation of magnets, he says:.

I really can’t do a good job, any job, of explaining magnetic force in terms of something else you’re more familiar with, because I don’t understand it in terms of anything else you’re more familiar with.

Feynman was also quoted as saying:.

I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.

Pretty interesting thing to hear from a guy who won a Nobel Prize for explaining quantum mechanics better than anyone ever had before. Even when he died in 1988 at the end of a long and fruitful careeer, a note at the top of his blackboard read:.

What I cannot create, I do not understand.

Vibecoding an inference chip

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ankitg

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that or rather, I vibe-coded an FPGA into running an LLM.
  • In a recent development, one of the more entertaining things about programming recently is that coding agents let me work in entirely newly introduced domains by giving me access to new programming languages and paradigms.
  • Recent findings suggest that I overheard some founders recently talk about how FPGAs work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that or rather, I vibe-coded an FPGA into running an LLM. And it… just worked.

In a recent development, one of the more entertaining things about programming recently is that coding agents let me work in entirely newly introduced domains by giving me access to new programming languages and paradigms. Lately, that has meant hacking on hardware, now that writing low-level software is much easier. So, in this blog post, I’m going to try to recount the experience of vibe coding an FPGA, going through a series of “oh shit” moments several times, and giving myself a new appreciation for what’s possible if you have a large token budget (thanks YC) and interesting problems to point the models at.

Recent findings suggest that I overheard some founders recently talk about how FPGAs work. I’ll admit I was relatively naive about them. I’d never really experimented with them in my startup or in college, so I knew little about them before. The basic idea I was familiar with: you can program a circuit into a reprogrammable chip. So rather than having a general purpose computing architecture (like a CPU) you can have a reprogrammable one, i.e. the configuration loaded onto the chip determines how its logic and routing are connected, and that (in theory) enables performance advantages. I also know that it took a mountain of C++ to write and involved manually analyzing waveforms for simulation and verification. I had never done this before though and it seemed cumbersome.

That’s about what I knew going into this.

Recent findings suggest that naturally, my ML brain thought “could we use these for AI inference”. I’m not the first to think this — there are a few repos attempting to port ML models to FPGAs on Github. But I hadn’t actually seen a writeup on whether coding agents are good at writing the low level C++ and Verilog code to program them and verifying the outputs so that they actually run accurately. (Spoiler alert, they are incredible at programming them.).

Sources indicate that so I decided I needed to get my hands on one. AWS has F2 instances with FPGA hardware, and that seemed easier than going and buying physical hardware, so I asked Codex to spin up a reservation and got cooking. It had a relatively limited memory of 16 GB of FPGA HBM. Around the same time, I was working with the DeepGrove founders who were discussing their new ternary weight architecture that is well suited for memory limited cases. It’s SOTA on Mac hardware with actual agentic tool calling, so I figured why not, let’s see if I can get this working on an FPGA and fast enough to be useful.

It has been revealed that what followed was a cloud agent running in Conductor for several days with me mostly just encouraging it periodically while it both (1) got a model fully running and (2) increased its speed by 33× from the first full-model bit-exact baseline to get it to a real-time relevant speed. It was one of the most mind blowing autoresearch loops I’ve run, ultimately writing roughly 3M lines across the experiment history and parsing 30M lines of output files, burning only $10,000 in Claude and OpenAI tokens to run hundreds of experiments. Most of the code is C++ and some Verilog. It’s been probably a decade since the last time I wrote any serious amount of C++ and I’ve never written Verilog. I honestly don’t know the first thing about Verilog. Most of my prompts were not particularly clever: they consisted mostly of me saying things like “you’re a superintelligent model, time to be more creative” and “let’s go for 2x faster, you got this”. Sometimes I brought some ML knowhow like “hey it’s time to consider speculative decoding” or “why is that running on CPU, you should port it”. But for the most part, it was just vibes and I’m pretty sure that with enough time the model would have figured out those things. Also, it seemed that both Astra and Opus (upcoming Fable wasn’t out yet) were pretty capable at this and I could use them interchangeably. I’m sure someone has a good benchmark for which is smarter but both passed my smart-enough threshold.

Measured benchmark tokens/s · select a step to see what changed.

A head loader that reads both of its memory banks at once (+17.3%, measured on and off on one image), a runtime expert-prefetch policy, and the router-job timing fix; run one clock step lower (225/425 MHz) after a soak test found random faults at 231.25.

The chart follows the measured optimization sequence: 6 → 213 tokens/s, or 33× the baseline.

At one point, around when it got to 10 TPS, I messaged the DeepGrove founders about this, and they replied surprised that it was working so easily, saying they had tried this a few months back and the models were not quite good enough to be particularly effective. They sent me a prompt that summarizes some of their lessons and I copy-pasted it into my session to see if it’d matter. It was essentially the most significant piece of actual guidance I added to this session. The prompt is reproduced below.

Sources indicate that here is what someone else did for a dense bs=1 decode optimized fpga implementation for a dense qwen style model with ternary weights. you should take this with a grain of salt and pick things that you believe are acutally useful to add to your plan. Please also dont do things if you dont think is useful that take a lot of times like runnning really long test of a cycle accurate simulation etc or like physical design since those can take like hours. here are some ideas please pick and choose use this as context and not somehting that you shoudl be strictly guided by somethings that could help. prioritiize speed of like getting this up and running though..

In a recent development, the coding agent diligently considered these asks, but it didn’t seem to make all that much of a difference qualitatively. Indeed, when I asked it later to read all of the logs and determine which of these instructions it actually used, it said:.

In a recent development, its biggest design ideas were already in my strategy before you pasted it. You pasted it on Oct 29 at 21:50 UTC: 4,741 characters describing what someone else did for a dense, batch-1, ternary FPGA decoder. Within 70 seconds I had sorted it into ten ideas to adopt and five to reject, and written that into every design agent’s brief. The shorter remark from your friend Edward, about using lookup tables as logic gates, came 24 minutes earlier and left nothing on the speed line.

Design ideas I adopted: mostly confirmation.

Already planned: streaming weights straight into the compute lanes, running rows in parallel, and reading the attention cache in bursts were all in the design brief I’d debuted 35–40 minutes earlier.

Ideas I rejected: all five numerics shortcuts. Lower-precision activations, a deferred norm, an 8-bit KV cache, online softmax and 16-bit probabilities each change the output bits. That is where their design got its efficiency, and your bit-exact rule ruled it out.

Process advice: this changed things right away.

What you asked: not to do things that take hours.

What I stopped: a simulation that had run for about 24 hours, and two 250 MHz builds.

What I switched to: a short loop of C tests, synthesis and a logic-depth check, with one place-and-route per integration.

Likely gain: it got hardware results sooner.

Possible cost, which I can’t prove: two hangs that only RTL simulation could show reached the board the next day, and the big integration lost 38 hours to them.

Sources indicate that one real find it triggered. While checking their memory ideas, I found AWS’s own reference memory design, which reaches 426 GB/s across all 32 memory channels. The memory subsystem was built from it.

In other words, for most of the actual design ideas it is unclear but there is good reason to believe the model would have figured them out, especially because it came up with them many cycles later after several compaction cycles. But the process advice was useful immediately for getting to hardware results sooner and increasing iteration speed. In other words, the humans are still useful at defining how to iterate fast and what correctness looks like, and the agents are great to manage the exploration.

It has been revealed that here are the changes the autoresearch loop found. Interestingly, it’s mostly a series of modest improvements that compound 1.5x ish every time, rather than one or two giant ones.

Baseline: the first full-model bit-exact FPGA image (R8), served with host-side prefix caching.

Host software only: per-command overhead fell from ~10 ms to 0.9 ms (persistent register mapping, streaming reads, no per-command SDK calls or fsyncs).

1.25× this step · 1.25× from baseline.

A 128-lane attention engine that reads the KV cache in bursts instead of a word at a time, keeping the reference's exact summation order.

1.74× this step · 2.18× from baseline.

A parallel MoE router with an exact GCC-sort tie-breaker plus a streaming output head with built-in argmax; moderate-effort routing let it run at 250 MHz.

1.46× this step · 3.19× from baseline.

A glue engine that parallelizes norms, RoPE, quantization and copies between engines in certified exact orders.

1.47× this step · 4.70× from baseline.

The full new pipeline (streaming ternary projection lanes + a new sequencer replacing R8's control path), after fixing two hangs that only appeared in hardware.

1.63× this step · 7.65× from baseline.

Exact speculative decoding: the host drafts tokens by prompt lookup and the FPGA verifies several in one pass.

1.04× this step · 7.97× from baseline.

Fixed a relay that moved router weights between dies at 1/6 speed: router stall per layer 43,862 → 12,292 cycles.

1.14× this step · 9.08× from baseline.

Head shadow v2 (start the next token on a provisional guess; catch misses early) plus cross-die timing fixes, enabling 237.5 MHz kernel / 450 MHz memory.

1.62× this step · 14.68× from baseline.

Exact speculative decoding with a real draft model: a cut-down Maple on the F2's host CPUs drafts ahead, and the FPGA verifies every token.

1.12× this step · 16.42× from baseline.

Doubled the memory ports from 4 to 8 (two projection lanes, output head striped across banks): 1.39× per clock, but congestion cut the clock to 181/375 MHz.

1.03× this step · 16.91× from baseline.

Hid the attention engine's KV fetches behind its compute, and replaced the router's 2,048-step serial sum with an exact order-independent one (12,292 → 2,338 cycles per layer).

1.24× this step · 20.98× from baseline.

Lossless 5-trit weight packing (−20% weight bytes), shorter serial steps, and moving the output head to the far die, which relieved congestion and allowed 225/400 MHz.

1.27× this step · 26.63× from baseline.

Re-speculation after head-shadow misses, speculative MoE expert prefill during the router, and a die rebalance (without the unused DDR controller) that ran 231.25/450 MHz on both boots.

1.08× this step · 28.63× from baseline.

A head loader that reads both of its memory banks at once (+17.3%, measured on and off on one image), a runtime expert-prefetch policy, and the router-job timing fix; run one clock step lower (225/425 MHz) after a soak test found random faults at 231.25.

1.16× this step · 33.13× from baseline.

Industry observers note that it’s difficult to do a 1:1 comparison across these configurations. I didn’t run the same autoresearch loop on every alternative, and I assume there is more performance to extract if I did. The point is to show how slow the FPGA was in its first implementation, and how far the optimization loop took it.

Recent findings suggest that the measurements below are from November 15 on AWS, replaying the same 8-chat × 3-turn benchmark. Prices are the on-demand rates recorded with that experiment. “Exact turns” counts outputs that matched the pinned CPU reference. The GPU implementations are included for context but did not satisfy the same bit-exact criterion but are pretty close in practice.

According to recent reports, this is one generation starting with a 16-token prompt and continuing until the 8,192-token context is full: 8,176 generated tokens. The five middle columns show decode speed in tokens/s at the indicated context length for several generations of iteration. The last column is wall-clock time for the whole run/.

It has been revealed that * For r8 and r9, the first two columns come from separate, shorter runs generating 2,032 tokens. The other columns come from the full-context run.

r9 improves short-context speed, while the complete long-context run is roughly tied with r8.

These examples come from the final r9 image.

246 tokens · 229.7 tokens/s · 1.16 s end to end.

Sources indicate that system prompt: “You are a helpful assistant. Think briefly before you answer, then reply clearly and concisely.”.

Industry observers note that this was a fun project. I’m not sure I’m ever going to use this specific chip architecture in this specific way, and I’m certainly not claiming that an 8,192-token-context model running on an FPGA is the way I’d recommend anyone use something like this in production. But it’s pretty epic that this just works. Capability like this completely shifts the overton window for what a committed team of engineers can work on. It should mean that entirely new types of ideas (scientific discoveries, products, startups) are possible if you can point the models in the right direction. I’m excited to see what everyone builds.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5bn.
  • Applied Compute was founded last year by three former OpenAI researchers.
  • “Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” noted Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and chief executive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Palo Alto Networks’ office in Singapore.

Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5bn. The startup helps companies train and run their own versions of open-weight AI models. Palo Alto announced the deal on Wednesday, minutes after The Wall Street Journal’s Kate Clark reported it.

Applied Compute was founded last year by three former OpenAI researchers. Earlier this month it raised $350m at a $3.25bn valuation, the Journal reported. It also stated it had reached $100m in run-rate revenue. Its co-founder and chief executive, Yash Patil, will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer when the deal closes. The deal still needs regulatory clearance and should close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027.

“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” noted Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and chief executive.

Open-weight models let users download and change the weights, the numbers that set how a model behaves. Palo Alto said no large provider offers them securely today. It plans to let companies train, adapt and run them in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments. Applied Compute will keep serving its own customers, and Palo Alto will sell the platform to its own base.

Industry observers note that arora told the Journal the deal means “venturing outside of cybersecurity”. On the earnings call, he stated open-weight models now carry more than 60% of token traffic. A year ago it was under 5%.

“If it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity. This could be bigger than what we do,” Arora stated on the call.

Sources indicate that palo Alto told analysts it expects the deal to add more than $1bn in annual recurring revenue by fiscal 2029. It prepares to build more than 100 megawatts of inference capacity. Capital spending on that will stay under $3bn through fiscal 2030, it said.

Arora also addressed whether Applied Compute’s team will stay. Its staff have “millions of reasons” to stay for the next three to four years, he wrote on X. They will keep their offices and, for the most part, their independence.

Sources indicate that the deal came with Palo Alto’s fiscal first-quarter results. Revenue rose 39% to $3.44bn in the three months to 31 October. Annual recurring revenue from its next-generation security business rose 66% to $9.73bn. Net income was $482m, up from $334m a year earlier.

Recent findings suggest that palo Alto raised its forecasts for the year. It now expects revenue of $14.52bn to $14.57bn. It sees adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 a share.

On the call, Arora linked part of that demand to the recent run of outages. He blamed them partly on IT teams rushing to patch AI-found flaws. He has argued before that AI prices must fall for the technology to take off. He has also called slowing AI down unrealistic.

Industry News: Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions.
  • While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”.

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”.

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:.

In fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

Sources indicate that the law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

Tech Report: UK can’t keep its Apple encryption order secret, tribunal rules

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the UK government can no longer keep its Apple encryption order secret, a tribunal has ruled.
  • The order is a technical capability notice under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016.
  • “Anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the three judges wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the UK government can no longer keep its Apple encryption order secret, a tribunal has ruled. The Home Office had argued that confirming the order would damage national security. The Investigatory Powers Tribunal rejected that claim in a judgment on Thursday.

The order is a technical capability notice under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. Such notices can require companies to change how their services work so the authorities can get access to data. Until now the Home Office had refused to confirm or deny it had served one on Apple.

“Anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the three judges wrote.

Industry observers note that the judges said the government had not kept to its own secrecy policy. The Times and the Financial Times had reported that government sources confirmed the order. The tribunal found that those briefings took place, and that ministers, senior officials or special advisers authorised them.

In a recent development, the Home Office noted leak investigations had found no source, but it gave the tribunal no details of them. The government had also let Apple brief senior US officials. The judges called that a further clear departure from its policy. They noted that the answer could be found by typing the question into Google’s chatbot.

According to recent reports, the ruling does not make the order’s content public. The judges agreed that publishing all the material would damage national security. But that does not mean every detail must stay secret, they noted. The tribunal will decide that question later.

Industry observers note that the parties expect a full hearing in the first half of 2027. Much of it can now take place in public, the judges remarked. Apple has five grounds of challenge. The tribunal can decide the first two entirely in public. One asks whether the power can reach interception outside the UK. The other asks whether it can be used to regulate the security a company offers its customers.

Apple welcomed the decision as a step in the right direction for public access to the case, Bloomberg reported. Caroline Wilson Palow, legal director of Privacy International, called it a “major victory” for transparency. Privacy International and Liberty brought a separate challenge with two individuals. Liberty called the result a victory for transparency.

In a recent development, the Home Office said the ruling was procedural. Apple has helped police and intelligence agencies for years, and the notice simply requires that it keeps the ability to do so, it said in a statement published by The Register.

“Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies,” a government spokesperson noted.

Apple filed its second claim in July, after the tribunal dismissed its first. In February 2025 it withdrew Advanced Data Protection for UK users. The feature extends end-to-end encryption to iCloud backups and more. Meta, TikTok and X also challenged UK data demands this autumn, from Ofcom, and reportedly lost.

Rumors about next year’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models have been ramping up, and they suggest Apple is designing an ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ that combines traits from two current models.

Apple keeps expanding the iPhone line to include new models. And while it’s great that there are more models for differing preferences and needs, it’s also left me missing the days of having one model that was the clear “best.”.

That problem isn’t going away, since the iPhone Duo represents a brand new type of iPhone that some customers will love, while others find it isn’t for them.

Recent findings suggest that with my failed iPhone Duo experiment over, I’m back to using iPhone 18 Pro as my default model. But I still have an iPhone Air around for work, and every time I pick it up, I’m struck by how impressive it remains.

I used the iPhone Air all of last year and loved it. The main reason I upgraded to an iPhone 18 Pro is the camera system. I have young children at home—including newborn twins—and want to capture the best possible photos before they get older.

iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera has been fantastic, and it’s great having the Telephoto again too.

But I still sorely miss the overall design of the iPhone Air. And it sounds like next year, I could get the best of both models.

Rumors indicate Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models will have a unique new design featuring a quad-curved display that makes it look bezel-free.

The new models are expected to also be a bit slimmer, use curved edges, and possibly even bring back titanium. Leakers say the new design borrows a lot from the iPhone Air’s look.

This sounds like exactly what I’ve been hoping for.

While the ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ certainly won’t—and shouldn’t—be as thin as iPhone Air, if it can slim down a little and adopt several other Air design traits, I suspect it will evoke the same affection the Air has.

But unlike the Air, the new Pro model will still offer the best camera system in an iPhone (not to mention better battery life).

Sources indicate that as a huge fan of the design of the Air, and the functionality of the 18 Pro, Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone model could prove the perfect model for me. And for anyone else not opting for iPhone Duo 2.

What do you think of the rumored iPhone 20 Pro design? Let us know in the comments.

DreamCoder: Coding harness and IDE from the author of Mastering Emacs

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Masteringemacs

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that.
  • It’s called DreamCoder, an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already.
  • I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs.

It’s called DreamCoder, an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already.

I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold.

Sources indicate that one thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents.

Why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like.

Recent findings suggest that but a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal.

So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build.

And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be.

Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it.

Let’s roll back time to the 1950s.

Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history.

It has been revealed that john McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the Advice Taker, a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called commonsense reasoning using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI.

Recent findings suggest that in the 50s there was little in the way of computer software that could do this. To formalize such a system you need a lot of data, rigorously formatted, and a method of manipulating the data. The data and code itself may intertwine recursively, and so an ordinary programming language would not work.

Sources indicate that to help him achieve this, McCarthy created the LISt Processing (LISP) language made up of two facets: M-expressions, a functional language in the vein of Algol; and S-expressions, designed for symbolic data representation, and never intended as a method of writing code. S-expressions were dolled up with parentheses. M-expressions meanwhile used square brackets to visually separate the two. Uniquely, the language specification had an eval feature that would prove that the language is also a universal Turing machine… if only McCarthy had the means to do so. It was theoretical because McCarthy lacked, in time, staff and money, what he needed build this recursive evaluator that can take as input its own world state and evaluate it alongside newly introduced expressions, a fact made even more apparent by the sheer complexity of his M-expression language and the limited resources he had at the time.

Steve Russell who worked with him proved him wrong the way most young people do: by just doing it. Russell wrote the first LISP Interpreter with a working eval function, but M-expressions got sidelined; the imperative, procedural nature of programming got squished into S-expressions instead. They had to hand roll the language on paper then punch it into cards and then batch run them. Eliding M-expressions was a simple matter of pragmatism. And so LISP was born. And through several accidents of history, M-expressions never gained traction. M-expressions live on in Wolfram’s Mathematica, but few other places.

Much later, McCarthy eventually conceded that,.

“One can even conjecture that LISP owes its survival specifically to the fact that its programs are lists, which everyone, including me, has regarded as a disadvantage.”.

In a recent development, S-expressions were always intended as the storage format with a bridge language to manipulate them. But by pushing evaluation into the same symbolic representation format as the data, we have what we call LISP today. That is why LISP is so unique. Consider a simple calculator. (+ 2 2) can simultaneously represent an expression that we want to compute, two plus two, or perhaps a ledger of record of a calculation we have already done.

McCarthy never built the Advice Taker in its purest form. He and his team ran into many philosophical, mathematical and computational walls that kept them occupied for a long time.

Sources indicate that the idea behind the Advice Taker was simple. If you want to go somewhere in your car, you can symbolically express this by building a chain of narrative facts – kinda like a flowchart, but as small snippets of rules and facts, not as one grand design.

The system would automatically resolve ambiguities, and all the logician had to do was capture the microcosm of the world he wished to represent:.

And so on. If you’re a student of Computer Science you’ll see echoes of Prolog here. The intent was simple: if we can symbolically express the world around us, we can advise that symbolic world with real-life facts, and have the automaton that uses this reified symbolic world change with it.

Sources indicate that but the axiomatic complexity of a world model would never survive an encounter with a 3-year-old child. Every axiom you write begets a newly introduced one — so you can walk to your front door? Well what if the door is locked? Or what if your car is parked on the street and not in your drive way?

A rules-based order of the world is a tender, beautiful one; but it is hard to build. It’s a fractal of ever-more specific and pedantic rules that conspire against you, just as you think you have a soluble world, typed and ready.

Anyone who has ever written Prolog knows exactly what that feels like!

In a recent development, I have my own personal story to add to this. In the 90s as a teenager I got a summer internship at a business that built banking software. They clearly didn’t know what to do with us teenaged interns, so on our first day they crammed us in a room and split us into teams and told us to build a flow chart for assembling a bike. Team exercise or something. Best one wins. We were told to be as specific and explicit as possible and account for as many conditions as we could think of, and the poor employees who had to mind us did their best to help. I distinctly recall losing because in my flowchart I forgot to open the box the disassembled bike came in.

McCarthy meanwhile eventually moved on and set up his own AI lab at Stanford, but the idea of the Advice Taker lived on.

In the late 70s Stallman and Steele create EMACS (Editing MACroS), also at MIT’s AI Lab, a set of building blocks on top of TECO, a famously inscrutable text editor. TECO did not update the screen by default; you had to toggle that on and hope your edits worked. You typed out terse keyboard commands, crossed your fingers and hoped you got it right, and then you patiently waited for your text manipulation to take effect. Rinse and repeat until you got what you wanted.

Industry observers note that stallman and Steele wanted more: they wanted macros so they could automate tedium of typing all that line noise. This strand of augmentation and later on self-modification is of course a unifying theme in Emacs today. The history of Emacs is long; but its outcome is known to us. I am typing this very article in Richard Stallman’s Emacs.

Industry observers note that mcCarthy’s Advice Taker left its mark in a subtle but indelible way. Warren Teitelman built the ADVISE system in his thesis with a cool title that reads like something out of a pulpy 1970s sci-fi novella: PILOT: A Step Toward Man-Computer Symbiosis. Teitelman, he later stated, was deeply inspired by McCarthy’s original idea of advising systems.

In a recent development, in his thesis, he describes a method of arresting a function call and inserting code before or after it is run. He was tired of editing other people’s LISP code by hand, and wanted a way of modifying their code without touching it directly. He built and rebuilt his system several times over the years, culminating in his ADVISE system in Interlisp, a structured editor and language runtime for manipulating LISP code and data. Interlisp eschewed plain text files; instead, you manipulated the tree at a high level of abstraction with explicit instructions like “move X list to Y position”. You can see my own attempts at merging structured editing with plaintext editing in Combobulate.

Sources indicate that MIT AI hackers eventually implemented Teitelman’s ADVISE system from his PILOT thesis in their own versions of Emacs. Later, it was canonized in Chalupsky’s own 1992 re-implementation in Emacs Lisp that lives on (M-x find-library advice.el) as one of Emacs’s advice systems to this day.

Sources indicate that what began as an idea for expressing automata using symbolism in an as-yet theoretical language in the 1950s culminated in a system for dynamically altering functions in GNU Emacs in the 1990s. What an unlikely lineage and history.

It has been revealed that symbolism and AI did not end with advising functions. There were many attempts at symbolic intelligence. Terry Winograd’s SHRDLU; Marvin Minsky’s Frame Systems; and even Emacs’s ELIZA-style M-x doctor all make use of symbolic “AI”.

None of them brought us closer to the AI that proponents of symbolic AI hoped they would.

In hindsight that seems obvious.

Recent findings suggest that writing a LISP macro just so will not produce artificial intelligence; nor will a carefully crafted web of rules and symbolic algebra suddenly spark intelligence. We know that today, but for a generation of computer scientists it felt like the future we have all read about in science fiction novels: a perfect, logical intelligence. A positronic brain. Robby the Robot; HAL 9000; C-3PO; Data; or the Speedies and Cuties from I, Robot. The unifying theme of these science fiction stories is they are automatons that follow strict rules — they obey Asimov’s three Laws of Robotics.

Every turn of hardware and software brought them ever closer to one day realizing the vision of an artificial intelligence, captured in neat axioms and LISP S-expressions, and modified in tools like Emacs.

It is surprising that symbolic AI, the vanguard movement for artificial intelligence, would instead dissipate into the wider body of Computer Science and programming as tools, languages and concepts, but not survive as a viable method of achieving AI.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps we always knew. Because at some point – even if we never really fully internalized it – we discovered that a ductile system that is shaped by its master’s desires is a tool that survives the ages because it remains eternally useful.

A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence.

For all the mathematical purity, beauty even, of the idea of a clockwork mind that is introspectable and malleable and its behavior expressed as S-expressions and interpreted by elegant algorithms and honed macros, we can, through the benefit of hindsight – now that we do have AI through other means – see that it was not to be.

The argument in favor of ductility is especially poignant when you learn of the Connectionists, which sounds like a bad 1960s band, but was in fact a loose coalition of people who believed firmly that neural networks, not symbolic AI, were the path to success. The Connectionist viewpoint was deeply unpopular in AI academia of that era, and funding for it was scarce.

Frank Rosenblatt invented the Perceptron, a foundational concept in neural networks, in 1957. Before Rosenblatt died in 1971, Marvin Minsky, an authority in the AI movement at MIT and a leading proponent of Symbolism, knifed the idea of Perceptrons and neural networks in a book he co-authored with Seymour Papert. They named the book, which they also dedicated to Rosenblatt, Perceptrons. The book deftly explains the mathematics of Perceptrons but undercuts their possible utility by showing that a single-layer Perceptron cannot represent an XOR gate. It was a deliberately obtuse reading of what neural networks could and could not do. With one additional hidden layer, a network can represent an XOR gate. It was a sneaky thrust of the stiletto: Minsky’s claims were overstated. A fact that was not lost on anybody in the Symbolic or Connectionist camps.

Sources indicate that it’s disputed if the Perceptrons book led to the first AI winter in the 1970s. It certainly did not help. But funding for many AI research paths dried up in the 1970s.

The Connectionist movement was vindicated in the long run. They lost the battle then, but they won the war, and the fruits of their research eventually gave us AI.

According to recent reports, the ductility we so prize in our software and tools today is antithetical to a strict, symbolic world model spun of axioms and facts that we hoped would one day birth AI. Yet to try and give birth to this world they had to build the most ductile tools of them all: LISP and, from that, also software like Emacs. The ultimate hacker’s tool.

It is ironic then that a neural network, a crude facsimile of how a brain works, a construct that is by its nature ductile and malleable, won out in the end.

So I feel a profound sadness that I started out programming DreamCoder in Emacs, the most extensible editor in the world, by hand back in May 2025, only to see DreamCoder write itself… in DreamCoder today.

It has been revealed that I am still sad, but I also know that our industry completely reinvents itself every decade or two. This is my second career upheaval. Most programmers today have not been around long enough to go through it themselves. So I feel for them that this especially massive quake is their first encounter with how unsentimental our industry is.

But for all the sadness, I wake up every day with a feeling of optimism that I have not felt in a very long time.

I finally get to build again, no longer weighed down by my decades of knowledge and experience that held my ambition in check. I truly have not felt this liberated since I was a teenager programming in Delphi, blissfully unaware that the things I was busy building were impossible for a self-taught teenager to ever realize. I see this reflection in others: the best programmers I know also love AI. Amateurs also revel in AI’s capabilities, happy that they can finally solve problems they could never afford to pay a programmer to do for them.

I must admit that building software has, over the years, gotten a lot more complex, with an ever-larger share of that work being repetitive tedium. This is more so with hobby software – as I do not get paid to do it, so I do not have a moral duty to see it through – where I’d do all the fun bits leaving just the enervating, boring and soul-crushing parts behind. Do you have a projects folder full of sad, abandoned projects like I do?

Now I can craft in abundance. AI has freed up a lot of toil but I somehow still find myself busy all day doing real work.

It has been revealed that building a coding harness is perhaps the closest I will get to the optimism all those researchers and scientists must have felt in the 1970s and 1980s. They hoped that with a little bit more work, their logical rules would kindle a newly introduced intelligence. Fifty years on, and I can simply tell DreamCoder to improve itself and watch as it changes before me. I can ask the AI running inside it to analyze the changes I have made to its tools and prompt and have it adjust them accordingly. It feels like science fiction; the very thing the researchers of yesterday strove to build. Yet we really do live in this reality now.

So. DreamCoder. Let me address the 900 lb gnu in the room: DreamCoder is not an Emacs-related application. The reason is unfortunately one of economics and access: I want to build an AI coding harness for everyone. But don’t worry: I have some cool looks for DreamCoder + Emacs, and AI + Emacs more generally going forward. So stay tuned.

But what about all those other coding harnesses? Well, most of those harnesses all suffer from the same mistakes. It is a problem that is not unique to coding harnesses or the people who make them, but a constraint we all labor under, and one that is not easily replaced by AI:.

Taste is a scarce, human resource.

And for all the bounty of AI, it still requires a human to persevere and to see things through. One thing intensive use of AI coding has taught me is that we’re going to need a lot of computer programmers who know what they’re doing going forward. I believe this is so, because let us be honest, most people do not want to program computers, even if that computer can actually do the bulk of the work for them. It requires a steady hand to build reliable software; that has not changed.

Therefore, if we programmers have to spend a lot of our time interacting with AI, then the tool we do it with should be ‘human-centric’ in its design, and it should take advantage of all the modern features we have at our disposal.

Back in May 2025 I took a look at all the tooling and remarked “no, thank you.” Today I look at the landscape and I feel pretty much the same.

In a recent development, and I think I am not the only one who feels that way. Most of these coding harnesses, to me, feel bristly. They shouldn’t be; but they are like that because we are at an notable inflection point where no one really knows what the future looks like. We’re all just… fumbling around a bit. It’s an exciting time to build software, even if we don’t quite know what the world will look like a few years hence.

It has been revealed that one thing I am adamant about is that DreamCoder must be a powerful, frontier-class coding harness. That means it should have all the features you’d expect from that: backgroundable sub agents, MCP servers, cache efficiency, and all that stuff. Check.

Industry observers note that but that stuff rapidly recedes into the background because, you know, it just works. Day to day you will dart between chats and terminals and whatnot, and you need an interface that accommodates that. Emacs is a tiling window manager; so is DreamCoder. DreamCoder’s window manager is a little bit cleverer than most window managers as every pane has a minimum, comfortable and maximum size. The window manager will therefore ensure windows always fit snugly on your screen, and you’ll never end up in a situation where windows are tiny and unreadable. It has a sophisticated constraint satisfaction solver that tries to balance your demand for a upcoming window (“open a terminal”) with the challenge of keeping your visible panes roughly the same size. If DreamCoder can’t wedge in a new pane, it’ll punt one to the hidden window bar. Just click it to resurface it, or hover it to see what it’s doing; it’s a live view.

Industry observers note that because of my Emacs roots, I think a good tool must be keyboard-friendly. Because it runs on a browser you get the mouse for free of course. But smacking the tab button over and over is a frustrating user experience in complex webapps, and doubly so a tiling window manager: where exactly are you going to end up when you tab from one window to the next? To combat that, I built an avy-style window and “point of interest” selector for chats. Tap a key and pick from a selection of “embark”-like actions such as clicking links or opening pictures. It’s a work in progress, but I think it works well.

Most high-volume operations like opening and creating panes is done through a Helm-like interface with search-as-you-type. It’s really efficient, of course. And it works with a mouse also; which is sort of the point. The keyboard’s there for those who want it, and the mouse for regular folk who are just getting started. One unique feature of the design, which admittedly I am still exploring privately, is that everything is stored as Javascript objects (on account of running in your browser) so it’s not too much of a leap to build “macros” that prefill most of these dialog windows, leaving behind just the fields you want to edit.

Industry observers note that but yeah. With DreamCoder I want to take the best of Emacs and its coterie of third-party packages and bring some of that with me. The world is still not ready for an Emacs-shaped future, sadly, so that is why DreamCoder is a standalone application and a web frontend.

Another thing that drives me wild: I see people with tmux running 10 claude codes (or codex, or…) cycling between them like a duck gallery at a carnival to see if one of them is done working, or if it needs human intervention.

So there’s two things to unpack here: one is running lots of things in parallel, and the other is observability. You need insight into what is going on: is an AI jammed because it’s awaiting an answer or a tool safety prompt? Perhaps you’ve parked a bunch of chats pending some conversations with coworkers or other work that must finish first.

Industry observers note that in DreamCoder you have workspaces. They’re like virtual desktops (or window configurations in Emacs lingo): a snapshot view of panes as you want em. As you can see from the screenshots, panes expand to fill all the space. So if you want more space, you can: resize them (with the mouse or keyboard); shuffle them to a named workspace; or float them so they sit on top of the other windows.

But if you’ve got a lot of things happening in multiple workspaces, it’s hard to keep tabs on that. That’s why DreamCoder has a substantial, honking minimap in the top-right corner. One for each workspace. The minimap is a miniature of your actual layout. Each pane in the map gently pulses when it’s working, and it makes it abundantly clear when it’s blocked. When there’s nothing to do, it’s green.

Because workspaces and panes are distinct things you interact with, it must be easy to navigate between them.

I also wanted full-on, optional Emacs key bindings, but that is… pretty much impossible to properly build. Browsers lock you out of some rather crucial Emacs button combinations. Sadly that feature is parked until I can solve it on all major browsers without breaking your normal browser keys.

Recent findings suggest that that’s not to say it doesn’t have Emacs-inspired key bindings. Most global actions are reachable with Alt+x, akin to M-x; local, pane-specific ones with Alt+c. Alt+m activates keyboard mode: you can now type the number of the named pane to jump to it; or WASD to switch the active pane in that cardinal direction.

Support for open weight models like Qwen, Gemma, Deepseek, GLM, etc. is also very key to me. They work so well. I’m really surprised, here in late 2026, just how capable small models are at local-only development compared to just one year ago. Qwen 3.8 27B, for example, is fantastically good for its size. You can do a lot of good software development with it if you’re a capable hand yourself. Bigger models equal more auto piloting; but that Qwen model? Wow. So local models work great. In fact I think the future is local for a lot of use cases. Intelligence is fast approaching a cost where it will be too cheap to meter. If you remember the personal computer revolution in the 1980s and 1990s, then there are definitely echoes of that here.

If you’ve been holding off on local models then I do recommend you reconsider. Small ones like Qwen 3.8 27B (or its cousin, Flash Next) can run well on a high-end gaming rig or Mac, or with a little investment if you do not have that. If you have a dinky old computer and you’re cash starved, then not all hope is lost. Turn to the potato agronomists on twitter: give twitter’s AI, Grok, what you have and what you can reasonably spend and tell it to track down the cutting edge setup for your rig. This is no lie the fastest, easiest way to catch up to the cutting edge of self-hosted inference today. Five minutes.

In a recent development, as I’ve been building DreamCoder, I have come to the belief I’m not just building a coding harness. Coding harnesses are an IDE for the future; it will do more than just display a chat window for coding agent work. DreamCoder does more than that already. It’s going the way of Emacs in that it’ll consume a wide range of adjacent workflows and tools. But I have only just gotten started. I am brimming with ideas I’m building in parallel, but they take time because as I noted it’s not about the code; it’s just one small facet of building something that works well. But you know that already: it’s always the last mile.

In a recent development, dreamCoder is the most ambitious, technically complex and advanced software project I have ever built in my life. And that’s just the beginning. I’m not done. I’ve barely started. I will be blogging about this going forward, in addition to my usual Emacs scribblings.

In a recent development, in fact, the thing I’m right now grinding away at is a world-class pentest and cybersecurity suite in DreamCoder. Every single bit of software we have ever written is vulnerable; we have many rough years ahead of us. Just look at the crippling vulnerabilities coming out every day now almost. Even the most security conscious person is going to find themselves on the wrong side for no other reason than we depend on packages that were mature and stable and assumed to be secure. DreamCoder can do its bit to help catch many of most obvious weaknesses, especially as new software is minted every day that also needs thorough testing.

To round it off, I would like to formally invite you to join me in making DreamCoder better by trying it out. It’s great. It’s not a toy; it’s not a demo; and it’s not a weekend prototype. It’s a frontier coding harness that has most of what you’d expect: MCP, backgroundable sub agents and shell commands, terminal windows, skills, hooks, 99% cache hit, it runs for days, and an interactive UI for all of it. There’s a handy dandy importer for your Pi, OpenCode or Codex configs also to help you get started. A couple of clicks and your model settings are set up in DreamCoder. Ready to go.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pavel Durov speaks at TechCrunch Disrupt Europe in Berlin in October 2013.

It has been revealed that telegram CEO Pavel Durov mocked Apple’s iPhone Duo on X, calling it “both too big and too small“, while announcing that Telegram now supports the foldable. The app switches to a two-column layout when the phone is opened.

Telegram has adapted its app for Apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, and its CEO used the moment to mock the device. “Apple finally made a phone that’s both too big and too small,” Pavel Durov wrote on X on Thursday.

Recent findings suggest that “It folds in half. Just like your enthusiasm,” he added.

Durov said Telegram still looked “incredible at both wrong sizes,” and joked that the company does “a lot of charity work.” He shared a short video of the app running on the foldable.

According to recent reports, when the phone is closed, Telegram looks like its usual iPhone version, Brazilian Apple site MacMagazine reported. Opened, it switches to a two-column layout like the iPad app, with chats on one side and the conversation on the other.

Sources indicate that the iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 and has a 5.4-inch outer screen and a 7.6-inch inner one. It sold out in minutes when preorders opened in October.

Industry observers note that reviewers praised the hinge but noted that many apps still needed updates for the bigger screen. Instagram chief Adam Mosseri said this week that designing for the Duo will be hard.

Durov has clashed with Apple before. In August, Apple briefly pulled Telegram from the App Store over a content violation. Durov remarked extortionists had found a way “to manipulate [Apple] into overreacting.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jolly, the mascot of Meta’s Muse AI agent.

Sources indicate that meta has put its Muse AI agent into a Chrome sidebar. Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, unveiled the Muse Chrome extension in a post on X on Friday. He remarked 200,000 people were already using it.

According to recent reports, muse browses in the user’s own Chrome and acts only inside its own group of tabs, Digital Trends reported from the Chrome Web Store listing. Meta notes Muse cannot see saved passwords, browsing history or Chrome settings. The listing also warns that Muse may take unexpected actions. Its activity may show up in a user’s Google account.

According to recent reports, the Muse Charm is a keychain-sized device for talking to the agent. Meta aims to charge $300 for it, The Information’s Jyoti Mann reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter. The Charm will come with up to 12 months of free 5G data from Verizon, according to the report.

Meta has delayed its smartwatch to next year to focus on the Charm, The Information reported. Mark Zuckerberg highlighted the device at Meta Connect in September and said it would ship in time for the holidays.

“We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon,” Meta’s Tyler Yee told The Information.

Sources indicate that some Instagram users are asking Muse to find and unfollow accounts that do not follow them back, WIRED’s Jason Parham reported on Friday. One user told WIRED he had heard of people losing their accounts for purging followers with third-party apps. He did not believe Muse could do it until he tried.

In a recent development, muse went live in Australia on Tuesday, Meta announced. Users can connect it to Gmail, Google Calendar, Instagram and OpenTable. Local partners such as Canva, Domain, Kogan, Officeworks and Ticketek will follow gradually.

“People stay in control, including choosing what Muse can access and approving purchases before they happen,” mentioned Meta’s Will Easton.

Industry observers note that muse has drawn 10 million users since its September launch. Meta says it runs on Muse Secure VM, a dedicated cloud computer. It keeps passwords and payment methods out of the agent’s view.

Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (280 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This repository holds the paper Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations by L.
  • The statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/.
  • The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This repository holds the paper Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations by L. Alpöge and T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it.

The statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/. Each comparator*.json pairs a statement file with Solution.lean, names the theorems whose statements must agree, and permits only the axioms propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice.

The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and time.

The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the paper states that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either.

The source of the paper is not in this repository.

It has been revealed that the package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes $(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$, one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled.

Tesla has started offering rides in its Cybercab in Dallas, the second city after Austin for the two-seater with no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla already runs Model Y robotaxis in Dallas and intends to start delivering Cybercabs to private buyers in Texas in December.

It has been revealed that tesla’s Cybercab, its two-seat robotaxi with no steering wheel or pedals, is now giving rides in Dallas, InsideEVs reported. “Cybercab has arrived in your city,” Tesla’s Robotaxi account posted on X on Thursday.

It has been revealed that tesla’s robotaxis also run in Houston, Fort Worth, San Antonio, Tampa, Orlando and Miami, mostly with the Model Y. It has focused on Texas and Florida, where the rules are looser than in states like California.

In a recent development, the US road safety agency, NHTSA, is looking into how Tesla decided a car with no wheel or pedals meets US safety rules. Unlike Amazon’s Zoox, Tesla did not ask for an exemption. NHTSA is also reviewing claims that Tesla robotaxis, including Cybercabs, sped in school zones.

Recent findings suggest that tesla is also starting to sell the Cybercab to some customers for $29,990. Owners must pay a $299 monthly fee, or the car will not run. The first cars should reach buyers in Texas in December.

To build more of them, Tesla aims to wind down Cybertruck output at its Texas plant around mid-2027.
